lessons.title: Horizontal circles and radial acceleration
lessons.summary: Connect angular speed to the actual inward resultant, including friction and smooth-surface normals.
lessons.objective: Convert angular speed and period, resolve the inward forces and check every contact or friction bound.
lessons.before: Review radians, resolving forces and Newton’s second law. The contact-force lesson explains normals and friction. A particle can accelerate even when its speed is constant.
lessons.ideas:
Direction changes while speed stays constant

For uniform motion on a circle of radius r, a turn through an angle in radians covers arc length r times that angle. Dividing by the elapsed time gives v=rω. Over a small turn, the equal-length velocity vectors form a similar triangle to the radius vectors. The velocity change divided by the elapsed time tends towards vω, directed towards the centre. Thus

\[\begin{gathered}v=r\omega\\a_r=\frac{v^2}{r}=r\omega^2\end{gathered}\]

The inward acceleration is not an extra force. It is produced by the inward resultant of the real forces: tension, friction, normal reaction or their components. Use the actual circle radius, which need not be a string length or a sphere radius.

Period and revolutions per minute

\[\begin{gathered}P=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\\\omega=\frac{2\pi n}{60}\quad(n\text{ in rpm})\end{gathered}\]

Angular speed is measured in radians per second. Period is time for one revolution, not the number of revolutions per second. Circular motion at constant speed has no tangential acceleration; non-uniform tangential dynamics is not needed in this chapter.

Draw forces before choosing an equation

\[\begin{gathered}\sum F_{\rm inward}=\frac{mv^2}{r}\end{gathered}\]

On a horizontal table, weight and vertical support can balance while horizontal tension or friction accelerates the particle. A stationary hanging counterweight has tension equal to its weight, but this equality is invalid if it accelerates. Two forces can oppose each other radially; use their signed resultant.

Friction provides a bound

\[\begin{gathered}|F|\le\mu N,\qquad N\ge0\end{gathered}\]

Find the friction required for the stated motion, then compare it with the available bound. On a flat turntable with no other vertical forces, N=mg. A sloping string changes N, so using μmg automatically can be wrong. Equality is justified at impending slip or when finding the minimum coefficient.

A horizontal circle inside a smooth bowl

Let the bowl radius be a, the height above its bottom h, and the downward distance from its centre z=a−h. Geometry gives r²=a²−z². The normal points towards the sphere centre, not towards the horizontal circle centre. Resolve it vertically and horizontally:

\[\begin{gathered}N\frac za=mg\\N\frac ra=mr\omega^2\\\omega^2=\frac gz,\qquad N=\frac{mga}{z}\end{gathered}\]

These formulas require a genuine horizontal circle with 0<h<a and positive normal reaction. The centre of the horizontal orbit lies on the vertical axis at the particle’s height.
lessons.method:
1. Find the circle centre, actual radius and relevant height geometry.
  2. Convert rpm or period to radians per second.
  3. Draw the real forces and resolve vertically and inward.
  4. Use the inward resultant equal to mv²/r, rather than adding a new force.
  5. Check normal signs, friction bounds, units and the stated steady-motion assumptions.
mistakes: Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration.
Do not add a separate centripetal force to a force diagram.
A sloping string length is not the horizontal circle radius.
Convert minutes to seconds before using rpm.
Friction is at its maximum only in a specified limiting state.

examples.title: 1 · One revolution connects three quantities
examples.question: A particle travels in a horizontal circle of radius \(\frac35\) m at 30 revolutions per minute. Find its angular speed, speed, inward acceleration and period.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\omega=\frac{2\pi(30)}{60}=\pi\\v=\frac{3\pi}{5}\\a_r=\frac{3\pi^2}{5}\\P=2\end{gathered}\]

The units are rad s⁻¹, m s⁻¹, m s⁻² and s respectively. The acceleration points inward even though the speed is unchanged.

examples.title: 2 · The coefficient needed on a turntable
examples.question: A 2 kg particle rests on a rough horizontal turntable, 0.8 m from its axis, and moves at 2 m s⁻¹ without slipping. Take \(g=10\) m s⁻². Find the required friction and the least possible coefficient.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}N=20\\F=\frac{2(2^2)}{4/5}=10\\\mu_{\min}=\frac{10}{20}=\frac12\end{gathered}\]

Static friction is inward. Coefficients greater than one half also permit this motion; equality is needed only for the least coefficient.

examples.title: 3 · The orbit radius differs from the bowl radius
examples.question: A particle moves in a horizontal circle inside a smooth hemispherical bowl of radius a, at height \(\frac a3\) above the bottom. Find its circle radius, angular speed and normal reaction.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}z=\frac{2a}3\\r=\sqrt{a^2-z^2}=\frac{\sqrt5}{3}a\\\omega^2=\frac{3g}{2a}\\N=\frac32mg\end{gathered}\]

The vertical component of the normal supports the weight. Its horizontal component supplies the radial acceleration around the vertical axis.

examples.title: 4 · A stationary counterweight sets the tension
examples.question: A 2 kg particle on a smooth table describes a circle of radius \(\frac34\) m. Its string passes through a smooth hole to a stationary 3 kg counterweight. Take \(g=10\) m s⁻². Find the angular speed and the rotation rate in rpm.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}T=30\\30=2\left(\frac34\right)\omega^2\\\omega=2\sqrt5\\n=\frac{60\sqrt5}{\pi}\end{gathered}\]

The counterweight is stationary, so its forces balance. The tabletop particle is accelerating horizontally, so its forces do not balance in that direction.

lessons.title: Conical pendulums, linked strings and elastic constraints
lessons.summary: Resolve the three-dimensional geometry into vertical balance and horizontal radial motion.
lessons.objective: Determine radii, tensions and angular speeds, checking that every string is stretched and can pull.
lessons.before: Complete horizontal radial dynamics. Review right-triangle geometry and Hooke’s law for a light elastic string. Elastic questions are cross-topic applications: the necessary law is also stated here.
lessons.ideas:
A conical pendulum has no vertical acceleration

For a particle of mass m attached by a taut string of length ℓ, let θ be its angle to the downward vertical. The particle moves steadily in a horizontal circle of radius r=ℓ sinθ, while its depth below the pivot is ℓ cosθ. Resolve the same tension in two directions:

\[\begin{gathered}T\cos\theta=mg\\T\sin\theta=mr\omega^2\\T=m\ell\omega^2\\\omega^2=\frac{g}{\ell\cos\theta}\end{gathered}\]

The cancellation of sinθ assumes a nonzero radius. Vertical hanging is not itself a nonzero circular orbit. For a taut ordinary string, 0<θ<π/2. Tension exceeds mg and the orbit radius is smaller than the string length.

Normals and additional strings change the equations

For a particle inside a cone whose generator makes angle α with the vertical, the inward normal has vertical component N sinα and horizontal component N cosα. Add any string force with its actual direction. With no other force apart from weight, N sinα=mg and N cosα=mrω². Use the cone geometry r=h tanα to relate radius to height.

Linked particles need separate force diagrams

A shared light string over a smooth guide has a common tension, but different particles can have different orbit radii, angular speeds and masses. For successive strings, the lower particle pulls the upper one outwards and downwards. Write both particles’ equations, rather than applying a single-pendulum formula to each without accounting for the connecting force.

Two strings can produce an inward sum

When a particle is joined to fixed points above and below its horizontal orbit, both strings pull inwards. Their vertical components oppose each other. Solve the vertical difference and radial sum, then check both tensions are non-negative. A negative lower tension means that string cannot remain taut.

An elastic length is an unknown

\[\begin{gathered}T=\lambda\frac{\ell-\ell_0}{\ell_0}\end{gathered}\]

Here ℓ₀ is natural length and λ is modulus, measured in units of force. For a conical elastic string, combine this law with T=mℓω² and T cosθ=mg. Find ℓ first, then the angle and radius. Reject any result with negative extension, cosθ outside its physical interval or an inconsistent hanging length.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the vertical axis and express each radius and depth geometrically.
  2. Draw a separate force diagram for each connected particle.
  3. Resolve vertically using zero acceleration and horizontally towards its own circle centre.
  4. Add any fixed-length, common-tension or elastic law constraints.
  5. Check all tensions, extensions, angles and unused geometric restrictions.
mistakes: The angle to the vertical and the angle to the horizontal are complementary.
The inward force is not the full tension when the string is sloping.
A common string tension does not imply equal angular speeds.
Use natural length in the denominator of Hooke’s law.
Negative tension is not a permissible compression force in a string.

examples.title: 1 · Geometry before the angular speed
examples.question: A conical pendulum has length \(13a\), and its string makes angle θ with the vertical, where \(\cos\theta=\frac{12}{13}\). Find its circle radius, tension, angular speed and speed squared.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}r=5a,\qquad T=\frac{13}{12}mg\\\omega^2=\frac{g}{12a}\\v^2=\frac{25}{12}ag\end{gathered}\]

The depth is 12a but the orbit radius is 5a. Neither can be replaced by the full length 13a in the radial acceleration.

examples.title: 2 · A horizontal orbit inside a cone
examples.question: A particle circles inside a fixed smooth cone at height h above its vertex. The generator makes angle α with the upward axis, with \(\tan\alpha=\frac43\). There are no strings. Find the normal reaction and angular speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}r=\frac43h\\\frac45N=mg,\qquad N=\frac54mg\\\frac35N=mr\omega^2\\\omega^2=\frac{9g}{16h}\end{gathered}\]

The normal is perpendicular to the generator. Its vertical and inward components use sine and cosine respectively, because α is measured from the axis.

examples.title: 3 · Find the stretched length first
examples.question: A light elastic string has natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(4mg\). A particle of mass m forms a conical pendulum with angular speed \(\sqrt{\frac ga}\). Find the stretched length, extension, tension and radius.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}T=m\ell\omega^2=\frac{mg\ell}{a}\\T=4mg\frac{\ell-2a}{2a}\\\ell=4a,\qquad e=2a,\qquad T=4mg\\\cos\theta=\frac14\\r=\ell\sin\theta=\sqrt{15}a\end{gathered}\]

The resulting angle is real and acute, and the extension is positive. Using natural length as the orbit radius would satisfy neither geometry nor the force equations.

examples.title: 4 · Both strings must remain taut
examples.question: A particle of mass m is joined by two strings, each of length \(5a\), to points \(8a\) apart on a vertical axis. It circles in the mid-plane with angular speed \(\sqrt{\frac ga}\). Find both tensions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}r=3a\\\frac45(T_U-T_L)=mg\\\frac35(T_U+T_L)=3mg\\T_U=\frac{25}8mg,\qquad T_L=\frac{15}8mg\end{gathered}\]

Both tensions are positive. Each horizontal component is inward, while their vertical components have opposite signs.

lessons.title: Vertical circles: energy and signed radial forces
lessons.summary: Use one height convention to link speed, tension, reaction and complete-circle conditions.
lessons.objective: Combine energy with the signed radial equation, and distinguish strings, one-sided surfaces and bilateral guides.
lessons.before: Complete radial force models. Review conservation of mechanical energy for smooth motion with a fixed centre: tension or a smooth guide force is perpendicular to the instantaneous motion and does no work.
lessons.ideas:
Choose height and angle explicitly

Use upward height y from the centre of a circle of radius a. A point at angle θ to the upward vertical has y=a cosθ; an angle φ to the downward vertical gives y=−a cosφ. This convention prevents the same cosine sign being used on both halves of a diagram.

Energy determines speed, not the radial force

\[\begin{gathered}v^2=u^2+2g(y_0-y)\end{gathered}\]

This follows by equating one half mv² plus mgy at the two points. It applies while the same smooth fixed constraint holds. An impact or an external release can start a new stage; conservation of energy alone cannot determine the impulse in an inelastic collision.

Resolve towards the centre

For a tension T, or inward reaction N from an inside surface, weight has inward component mgy/a. Therefore

\[\begin{gathered}T+\frac{mgy}{a}=\frac{mv^2}{a}\\T=\frac{mv^2}{a}-\frac{mgy}{a}\end{gathered}\]

The same expression gives an inward signed reaction for a bead threaded on a wire. A negative value then means an outward reaction, which the wire can supply. An ordinary string and a one-sided inner surface cannot supply a negative value.

A useful dimensionless energy constant

\[\begin{gathered}K=\frac{u^2}{ag}+\frac{2y_0}{a}\\\frac{v^2}{ag}=K-\frac{2y}{a}\\\frac{T}{mg}=K-\frac{3y}{a}\end{gathered}\]

These are derived shortcuts, not new physical laws. They apply to one fixed radius and one energy stage. At the bottom, tension is (K+3)mg; at the top it is (K−3)mg. The greatest and least tensions differ by 6mg whenever a complete string circle is possible.

Reaching the top and keeping a constraint are different tests

For a string or inside one-sided surface, the limiting complete-circle condition is K≥3: the top speed squared is at least ag and the top tension is non-negative. From the bottom this becomes u²≥5ag. Equality allows zero tension at the top instant. A rigid light rod or threaded wire can sustain an outward radial force, so this string criterion must not be imposed on it. Check positive speed all the way round; a zero-speed unstable top state is not an ordinary completed revolution.

Change of centre starts a new geometry

If a string catches a smooth peg with no impulsive change of tangential speed, the new radius and centre must be used immediately afterwards. The speed is continuous, but the tension generally jumps because v²/r changes. Recompute the complete-circle condition using the new radius.
lessons.method:
1. Fix an upward height origin and identify the direction of the radial component of weight.
  2. Use energy to express speed at each requested point.
  3. Apply the inward signed force equation with the actual radius.
  4. For a complete orbit, check the whole arc, especially the top and bottom.
  5. For rods or wires, interpret a negative signed reaction correctly; for pegs, reset the centre.
mistakes: Energy gives speed but does not by itself give tension.
The weight component changes sign between the upper and lower halves.
Positive speed does not guarantee a taut string.
A threaded wire can push outwards; a string cannot.
After a peg catches, the speed can stay continuous while tension jumps.

examples.title: 1 · The top has a smaller force as well as a smaller speed
examples.question: A particle starts from the bottom of a vertical circle of radius a with speed \(\sqrt{8ag}\), attached by a string. Find its top speed, greatest tension and least tension.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=8-2=6\\v_{\rm top}^2=(6-2)ag=4ag\\T_{\max}=9mg,\qquad T_{\min}=3mg\end{gathered}\]

The minimum tension is positive, so the string stays taut throughout. The difference in tensions is 6mg, not the difference in kinetic energies.

examples.title: 2 · Opposite ends of an inclined diameter
examples.question: At a lower point A, \(y_A=-\frac35a\), a string-constrained particle has speed \(\sqrt{6ag}\). B is diametrically opposite A. Find its speed squared at B and \(T_A:T_B\), and check a complete turn is possible.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=6-\frac65=\frac{24}5\\v_B^2=\left(\frac{24}5-\frac65\right)ag=\frac{18}5ag\\T_A=\frac{33}5mg,\qquad T_B=3mg\\T_A:T_B=11:5\\T_{\rm top}=\frac95mg\gt0\end{gathered}\]

The speed difference uses the full height rise 6a/5. The radial weight components have opposite signs at the two endpoints.

examples.title: 3 · A complete interval under a force cap
examples.question: At height \(\frac a2\) above the centre, a particle has speed u. It must complete a string-constrained circle, allowing the limiting zero top tension, while the tension must never exceed \(9mg\). Find the complete interval for \(\frac{u^2}{ag}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=\frac{u^2}{ag}+1\\K\ge3,\qquad K+3\le9\\2\le\frac{u^2}{ag}\le5\end{gathered}\]

Both boundaries are included. The lower one tests the top; the upper one tests the bottom. Checking only the starting tension would miss the largest force.

examples.title: 4 · A threaded wire can reverse its reaction
examples.question: A bead is threaded on a smooth vertical circular wire. Its bottom speed squared is \(\frac92ag\). Find the speed squared and signed inward reaction at \(y=\frac9{10}a\). Can it complete the circle?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=\frac92-2=\frac52\\v^2=\left(\frac52-\frac95\right)ag=\frac7{10}ag\\R_{\rm inward}=\left(\frac52-\frac{27}{10}\right)mg=-\frac15mg\\v_{\rm top}^2=\frac12ag\gt0\end{gathered}\]

The reaction is outward with magnitude mg/5. A threaded wire can supply it, and the speed stays positive. A one-sided inner surface or a string would lose its constraint before reaching this point.

lessons.title: Slack strings, turning points and loss of contact
lessons.summary: Decide which event is reached first, with the correct sign for the surface reaction.
lessons.objective: Locate and justify a first loss-of-constraint event, including cases where a turning point prevents it.
lessons.before: Complete energy and signed radial forces. Distinguish an inner shell, an outer surface and a threaded wire. A vanishing force is an event condition, not permission to continue using circular equations afterwards.
lessons.ideas:
An ordinary string cannot push

While taut, the string force is inward. Use T≥0 along the actual path. On an upper ascent, the first possible slack point satisfies T=0, giving

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{y_s}{a}=\frac K3\\v_s^2=g y_s\end{gathered}\]

The point must lie on the circle, have a real positive speed, and be reached before any turning point or earlier loss event. An algebraic cosine outside [−1,1] describes no point on the circle. A zero tension only at the top in the K=3 limiting case does not imply a finite projectile interval.

Speed can vanish before tension does

Energy gives a candidate turning height y/a=K/2. If K<0 for an upward string launch from the lower half, this lower-half turning point is reached before the formal T=0 height K/3. At the turn the tension is −Kmg/2>0, so the particle reverses while the string stays taut. If 0<K<3 and the initial state permits ascent, loss occurs on the upper half with positive speed. Boundary cases must be analysed directly.

Outside a sphere, the normal points outwards

On the exterior, weight acts partly inwards but the surface normal acts outwards. With upward centre height y and the same energy constant K,

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{mgy}{a}-N=\frac{mv^2}{a}\\\frac N{mg}=\frac{3y}{a}-K\end{gathered}\]

For a top launch with speed u, K=u²/(ag)+2. Initial contact needs u²≤ag. During descent the normal decreases; at first loss y/a=K/3 and v²=gy. A launch faster than √(ag) is not an initially surface-following motion. A non-top start needs its own initial contact check.

Check the full arc, not only the event equation

For an inner constraint on ascent, T or N decreases as y increases. For an outer surface on descent, N decreases as y decreases. These monotonic relations help establish the first zero. Verify that all earlier points have a physically admissible force and non-negative speed.

After the constraint disappears

The particle starts free motion with the same position and tangent velocity. Its acceleration then is gravity alone; it no longer has acceleration v²/a towards the old centre. A string can become taut again or a particle can meet a surface again, so check which free-flight event occurs first.
lessons.method:
1. Write the valid circular energy and signed radial-force equations.
  2. Find candidate zero-force and zero-speed events.
  3. Check geometric domains and the order in which the particle reaches them.
  4. Confirm positive force on the preceding arc and interpret limiting top states separately.
  5. At genuine release, retain the tangent velocity and begin a free-flight model.
mistakes: A negative calculated tension does not describe a compressive string.
Do not continue circular equations through a projectile interval.
For an outer surface, the normal is outward.
A formal zero-force point can lie beyond a turning point.
Always verify initial contact before calculating a later loss point.

examples.title: 1 · Slackening before a complete turn
examples.question: A particle starts at the bottom of a string circle with speed \(2\sqrt{ag}\). Find the first slack point, its speed squared and the initial tension.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=4-2=2\\\frac{y_s}{a}=\frac23\\v_s^2=\frac23ag\\T_0=5mg\end{gathered}\]

On ascent, tension decreases from 5mg to zero. The release speed is positive and the height is below the top; the string does not complete the circle.

examples.title: 2 · An exterior surface has the opposite normal sign
examples.question: A particle is projected horizontally from the top of a smooth sphere with speed \(\sqrt{\frac{ag}5}\). Find the initial normal reaction, loss angle cosine to the upward vertical and speed squared at loss.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=\frac15+2=\frac{11}5\\N_0=\left(3-\frac{11}5\right)mg=\frac45mg\\\cos\theta=\frac{11}{15}\\v_s^2=\frac{11}{15}ag\end{gathered}\]

The initial normal is positive. As the particle descends, the exterior reaction falls to its first zero at this angle.

examples.title: 3 · A turning point blocks a formal slack point
examples.question: A particle starts at the bottom of a string circle with speed \(\sqrt{\frac32ag}\). Does it reach the height predicted by setting the tension to zero?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=\frac32-2=-\frac12\\\frac{y_{\rm turn}}a=\frac K2=-\frac14\\T_{\rm turn}=-\frac K2mg=\frac14mg\\\frac{y_{T=0}}a=\frac K3=-\frac16\end{gathered}\]

During ascent it reaches −a/4 first, where its speed is zero and the tension is still positive. It turns back; the higher formal zero-tension point is never reached.

examples.title: 4 · Work backwards from a required loss point
examples.question: A particle starts at a lower point with cosine \(\frac12\) to the downward vertical. Choose its upward tangential launch speed u so it first loses tension at cosine \(\frac45\) to the upward vertical. Find \(u^2\) and the initial tension.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}K=3\left(\frac45\right)=\frac{12}5\\\frac{u^2}{ag}=K+1=\frac{17}5\\\frac{T_0}{mg}=K+\frac32=\frac{39}{10}\end{gathered}\]

The required release has positive speed. Tension decreases with height from its positive initial value, so this is its first zero; K is below the complete-circle threshold 3.

lessons.title: Release, impacts and changes of centre
lessons.summary: Join circular stages to projectile motion or collision equations without carrying an invalid law across the event.
lessons.objective: Transfer position and tangent velocity accurately between stages, and use the correct impulse and energy laws.
lessons.before: Complete first release events and projectile components. Three written questions use direct collisions: momentum and Newton’s restitution law are stated below. Do not assume that kinetic energy survives an inelastic collision.
lessons.ideas:
Release preserves the tangent velocity

At a right-hand point (x,y) of a circle of radius a, anticlockwise motion has tangent velocity (−vy/a, vx/a), where v is the speed. Clockwise motion reverses both signs. Here the v in each component is the scalar speed, not a component label. Derive the direction from the diagram rather than memorising a sign.

\[\begin{gathered}(u_x,u_y)=\left(-\frac{vy}{a},\frac{vx}{a}\right)\\X=x+u_x t\\Y=y+u_y t-\frac12gt^2\end{gathered}\]

The free-flight clock starts at release. At maximum height, vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal velocity generally remains nonzero. Use y+u_y²/(2g) only if the particle is initially rising and no earlier contact interrupts the flight.

Ground impact and the first return to a surface

For a sphere resting on the ground, ground level is Y=−a relative to its centre, not Y=0. For a return to a circular surface, solve X²+Y²=a² and exclude the release root t=0. Verify there is no earlier positive contact and select the first admissible event. The radial equation from the previous stage is no longer valid in flight.

Collision equations start a new energy stage

For a direct impact along a common tangent, use signed velocities in one fixed direction. If the tension impulse has no component along that tangent, total momentum in that direction is conserved. For a rear particle approaching a stationary front particle,

\[\begin{gathered}m_1U=m_1V_1+m_2V_2\\V_2-V_1=eU,\qquad 0\le e\le1\end{gathered}\]

Restitution compares relative separation speed with relative approach speed. Kinetic energy is conserved for e=1; it decreases for an inelastic impact. For coalescence both particles have the same final velocity. Apply smooth circular energy separately before and after the impact using the appropriate moving mass and speed.

A smooth peg changes the radius

When a string catches a peg, the new centre and shortened radius alter the radial acceleration. If the tangent is unchanged and the ideal catch causes no speed impulse, speed is continuous. Compute the tension on each side of the event using its own radius and radial weight component. Test any proposed complete turn about the new centre separately.

Keep one timeline

State which clock and centre are used, label quantities immediately before and after each event, and check physical conditions on every stage. If a quadratic flight equation has two positive roots, the relevant root is not automatically the larger one: the preceding geometry decides.
lessons.method:
1. Finish the first circular stage up to the first valid event.
  2. Record the event position and signed tangent components.
  3. Use projectile equations, impulse equations or a new circle as appropriate.
  4. Restart energy with the new speed, centre, radius and moving mass.
  5. Check event order, contact conditions, physical roots and every requested output.
mistakes: The launch direction after release is tangent, not radial.
Ground level for a sphere resting on the ground is one radius below its centre.
Do not conserve kinetic energy across an inelastic impact.
Use signed rebound velocity in momentum and restitution equations.
A peg can change tension without changing instantaneous speed.

examples.title: 1 · A tangent release followed by a highest point
examples.question: A particle loses contact with the inside of a circle at its upper-right point with \(y=\frac a2\), while rising anticlockwise. Its release speed is \(\sqrt{\frac{ag}2}\). Find the signed velocity components and greatest height above the centre, before any further contact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\frac{\sqrt3}2a\\u_x=-\sqrt{\frac{ag}{8}},\qquad u_y=\sqrt{\frac{3ag}{8}}\\Y_{\max}=\frac a2+\frac{u_y^2}{2g}=\frac{11}{16}a\end{gathered}\]

The velocity points upwards and leftwards. The inward release condition v²=gy is satisfied. The apex occurs before the next circular contact; maximum height does not mean zero total speed.

examples.title: 2 · The ground lies below the sphere centre
examples.question: A particle leaves the upper-right exterior of a smooth sphere at \(y=\frac a2\), moving downwards with speed \(\sqrt{\frac{ag}2}\). The sphere rests on horizontal ground. Find the time from release to impact and the horizontal ground distance from the vertical axis.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x_0=\frac{\sqrt3}2a,\qquad y_0=\frac a2\\u_x=\frac{\sqrt2}4\sqrt{ag}\\u_y=-\frac{\sqrt6}4\sqrt{ag}\\-a=\frac a2-\frac{\sqrt{6ag}}4t-\frac12gt^2\\t=\frac{\sqrt6}2\sqrt{\frac ag}\\X=\frac{3\sqrt3}4a\end{gathered}\]

The other flight-time root is negative. On the outgoing flight the particle stays outside the sphere until it reaches the ground. Setting the target height to zero would stop the calculation at centre level.

examples.title: 3 · Rebound, then test the new circle
examples.question: A particle P of mass m reaches the bottom of its string circle with rightward speed \(4\sqrt{ag}\). It collides elastically with a stationary particle Q of mass \(3m\), directly along the horizontal tangent. Find both signed final velocities and P’s first loss-of-tension height.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}4\sqrt{ag}=V_P+3V_Q\\V_Q-V_P=4\sqrt{ag}\\V_P=-2\sqrt{ag},\qquad V_Q=2\sqrt{ag}\\K_P=4-2=2,\qquad y_s=\frac23a\end{gathered}\]

P rebounds to the left but has the same post-impact speed magnitude 2√(ag). The impact is elastic, so its total kinetic energy check agrees. P then ascends with a new energy constant and cannot complete the string circle.

examples.title: 4 · A peg makes the force jump
examples.question: A particle reaches the bottom of a string circle of radius a with speed \(2\sqrt{ag}\). The string catches a smooth peg a/3 below the old centre, with no instantaneous speed change. Find the tension just before and after, and test a complete turn about the peg.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}b=\frac23a\\T_-=m\frac{4ag}{a}+mg=5mg\\T_+=m\frac{4ag}{2a/3}+mg=7mg\\v_{\rm new\ top}^2=4ag-4gb=\frac43ag\\T_{\rm new\ top}=mg\gt0\end{gathered}\]

The tangential speed is continuous but the radial acceleration is larger immediately after the catch. The new top tension is positive, so the shortened string permits a complete turn.

questions.title: Angular speed, linear speed and period
questions.prompt_html: A particle circles at radius \(\frac{3}{4}\) m at \(20\) rpm. Give angular speed, linear speed, inward acceleration and period, in rad s⁻¹, m s⁻¹, m s⁻² and s.
questions.answer_html: Angular speed: \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\); Linear speed: \(\frac{\pi}{2}\); Inward acceleration: \(\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}\); Period: \(3\)
