questions.title: A radius inferred from two steady runs
questions.prompt_html:
A small bead is guided around a fixed horizontal circular track. In a first run it moves at a constant angular speed \(3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). In a second run its constant angular speed is \(5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). The radial acceleration in the second run exceeds that in the first by \(12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the radius of the track.

    [3]

  2. Find the distance travelled in 8 seconds during the second run.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For each steady run the radial acceleration is \(r\omega^2\). The same radius is used in both runs, so \[25r-9r=12.\] Thus \(16r=12\) and \(r=3/4\ \mathrm m\).

Part (b)

The speed is \(v=r\omega=(3/4)5=15/4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is constant during the run, so the distance is \((15/4)8=30\ \mathrm m\).
questions.hint_html: Compare the radial accelerations before finding the linear speed.

questions.title: Changing the radius at fixed radial acceleration
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves at constant speed in a circle of radius \(\frac32\ \mathrm m\), completing a revolution in \(\pi\ \mathrm s\). It is then moved to a circular path of radius \(6\ \mathrm m\), on which it also moves at constant speed.

  1. Find its radial acceleration in the first motion.

    [2]

  2. The radial acceleration is unchanged. Find the period of the second motion.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The angular speed is \(2\pi/\pi=2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Hence \(a_R=r\omega^2=(3/2)2^2=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Part (b)

The new angular speed satisfies \(6\omega^2=6\), so \(\omega=1\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Thus the new period is \(2\pi/\omega=2\pi\ \mathrm s\); the angular speed is not unchanged.
questions.hint_html: Equal radial accelerations do not imply equal angular speeds when the radii differ.

questions.title: Speed from a measured resultant force
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(\frac35\ \mathrm{kg}\) moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle of radius \(\frac54\ \mathrm m\). The resultant force on the particle has magnitude \(\frac{27}{5}\ \mathrm N\).

  1. Find the speed of the particle and state the direction of the resultant force.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For uniform circular motion the resultant force is radial and directed towards the centre. Using \(F=mv^2/r\), \[\frac{27}{5}=\frac{(3/5)v^2}{5/4},\qquad v^2=\frac{45}{4}.\] Speed is positive, so \(v=3\sqrt5/2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.hint_html: Use the mass and radius as well as the force.

questions.title: A tension measurement and revolutions per minute
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(3/2\ \mathrm{kg}\) moves at constant speed on a smooth horizontal table. It is attached to a fixed point on the table by a light inextensible string of length \(4/5\ \mathrm m\). The tension is \(12\ \mathrm N\).

  1. Find the rotation rate in revolutions per minute.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Tension supplies the radial force, so \(12=(3/2)(4/5)\omega^2\). Thus \(\omega^2=10\) and \(\omega=\sqrt{10}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). The rate is \(60\omega/(2\pi)=30\sqrt{10}/\pi\) revolutions per minute.
questions.hint_html: One complete revolution corresponds to 2π radians.

marking_criteria.description_html: Convert angular speed to revolutions per minute.

questions.title: Period from a specified tension
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves steadily on a smooth horizontal plane, joined to a fixed point by a taut light inextensible string of length \(2a\). The tension is \(9mg\).

  1. Find the time for one complete revolution.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The inward equation is \(9mg=m(2a)\omega^2\), so \(\omega=3\sqrt{g/(2a)}\). The period is \(2\pi/\omega=(2\pi/3)\sqrt{2a/g}\).
questions.hint_html: Convert angular speed to the time for 2π radians.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain angular speed from the radial equation.
Use period equal to 2π divided by angular speed.

questions.title: Finding a friction limit from a rotation rate
questions.prompt_html:
A particle rests relative to a rough horizontal turntable at a distance \(\frac54\ \mathrm m\) from its axis. The table turns steadily at \(\frac{36}{\pi}\) revolutions per minute. The particle is just about to slip. Take \(g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the table.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Convert the rate to radians per second: \[\omega=\frac{36}{\pi}\frac{2\pi}{60}=\frac65.\] There is no vertical acceleration, so \(N=mg\). Friction alone supplies the horizontal inward force. At the limiting rate, \[\mu mg=mr\omega^2=m\frac54\left(\frac65\right)^2.\] Cancelling \(m\) gives \(\mu=(9/5)/10=9/50\).
questions.hint_html: First convert the rotation rate to radians per second.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply limiting friction as the inward force.

questions.title: Two linked particles at an outward-slip threshold
questions.prompt_html:
Particles \(A\) and \(B\), of masses \(m\) and \(km\), rest relative to a rough horizontal turntable. They lie on the same radial line at distances \(a\) and \(3a\) from the axis and are joined by a taut light inextensible string of length \(2a\). The coefficient of friction for both contacts is \(1/4\). At angular speed \(\sqrt{g/(5a)}\), both particles are simultaneously on the point of slipping radially outwards. Here \(k\gt 0\).

  1. Find the tension in the string.

    [3]

  2. Find k and verify the friction direction for the outer particle.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For the inner particle, tension acts outwards but limiting friction acts inwards. Hence \[\frac14mg-T=ma\frac{g}{5a}=\frac15mg.\] It follows that \(T=mg/20\), which is positive.

Part (b)

On \(B\), both tension and friction point inwards. The required force is \(km(3a)g/(5a)=3kmg/5\), so \[\frac{mg}{20}+\frac14kmg=\frac35kmg.\] Thus \(1/20=7k/20\), giving \(k=1/7\). The required friction on \(B\) is \((3k/5-1/20)mg=mg/28\gt 0\), inward, and equals \(\mu kmg\).
questions.hint_html: The string pulls the inner particle outwards and the outer particle inwards.

marking_criteria.description_html: Choose the correct directions on the inner particle.
Form its radial equation at the friction limit.
Use both inward forces for the outer particle.

questions.title: Two levels in a spherical bowl
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside of a fixed hemispherical bowl of radius \(a\). In one motion its height above the lowest point is \(a/5\), and its angular speed is \(\omega_1\). In a second motion its height is \(a/2\), and its angular speed is \(\omega_2\).

  1. Find \(\omega_1/\omega_2\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(\theta\) be the angle between the upward vertical and the normal reaction. The horizontal circle has radius \(a\sin\theta\), not \(a\). Resolving gives \[N\cos\theta=mg,\qquad N\sin\theta=m\omega^2a\sin\theta.\] Thus \(\omega^2=g/(a\cos\theta)\). Since \(a\cos\theta=a-h\), \(\omega^2=g/(a-h)\). Consequently \[\frac{\omega_1^2}{\omega_2^2}=\frac{a-a/2}{a-a/5}=\frac58.\] Both angular speeds are positive, so take the positive square root.
questions.hint_html: Express the vertical distance below the centre as a minus the stated height.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the horizontal radius and radial equation.

questions.title: Circular motion inside a cone with a counterweight
questions.prompt_html:
A fixed hollow cone has its vertex \(O\) below its rim and has a smooth inner surface. Its semi-vertical angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan\alpha=4/3\). A light inextensible string passes through a small smooth hole at \(O\). A particle of mass \(2m\) hangs in equilibrium below \(O\). The other end is attached to a particle \(P\) of mass \(m\), which moves in a horizontal circle on the inner surface at height \(h\) above \(O\).

  1. Find the angular speed of P in terms of g and h.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The common tension is \(2mg\), acting along the sloping string towards the vertex. Here \(\sin\alpha=4/5\), \(\cos\alpha=3/5\), and the horizontal circle radius is \(r=h\tan\alpha=4h/3\). The normal force \(N\) acts upwards and towards the axis. Vertical balance gives \[N\sin\alpha=mg+2mg\cos\alpha,\] so \(N=(11/4)mg\). Resolving horizontally inwards, \[N\cos\alpha+2mg\sin\alpha=m\omega^2r.\] The left side is \((33/20+8/5)mg=(13/4)mg\). Hence \[\omega^2=\frac{(13/4)g}{4h/3}=\frac{39g}{16h}.\] The reaction is positive and the radius is nonzero, so the stated motion is admissible.
questions.hint_html: The tension has a downward component, but the normal reaction has an upward component.

questions.title: Choosing the physical level in a bowl
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves steadily in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside of a hemispherical bowl of radius \(a\). The bowl is fixed with its rim horizontal. The speed of the particle is \(\sqrt{21ga/10}\). Its height above the lowest point is \(h\), with \(0\lt h\lt a\).

  1. Find \(h\) in terms of \(a\).

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(c=\cos\theta=(a-h)/a\), where \(\theta\) is the angle of the normal reaction to the upward vertical. Then \(0\lt c\lt 1\), the horizontal radius is \(a\sqrt{1-c^2}\), and vertical balance gives \(N=mg/c\). The horizontal equation gives \[\frac{mg}{c}\sqrt{1-c^2}=\frac{mv^2}{a\sqrt{1-c^2}},\] so \(v^2/(ag)=(1-c^2)/c\). Substituting the given speed, \[10c^2+21c-10=0=(5c-2)(2c+5).\] The roots are \(2/5\) and \(-5/2\). Only \(c=2/5\) describes a point inside the lower hemispherical bowl. Therefore \(h=a(1-c)=3a/5\).
questions.hint_html: Use a cosine variable constrained to lie between zero and one.

questions.title: How the orbit height changes with angular speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside of a fixed hemispherical bowl of radius \(a\). Its height above the lowest point is \(h\), and its angular speed is \(\omega\). In a second steady motion the angular speed is \(\sqrt2\,\omega\) and the height is \(3h\). Both orbits lie below the rim.

  1. Show that \(\omega^2=g/(a-h)\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(h\), and state the normal reaction in the second motion for a particle of mass \(m\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the normal reaction make angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical. Its equations are \[N\cos\theta=mg,\qquad N\sin\theta=m\omega^2a\sin\theta.\] Eliminating \(N\) gives \(\omega^2=g/(a\cos\theta)\). Since \(a\cos\theta=a-h\), the required result follows.

Part (b)

The second motion satisfies \(2\omega^2=g/(a-3h)\). Combining with (a), \[\frac2{a-h}=\frac1{a-3h},\qquad 2a-6h=a-h.\] Thus \(h=a/5\); the second height \(3a/5\) is indeed below the rim. In that motion \(\cos\theta_2=1-3/5=2/5\), so \(N_2=mg/(2/5)=5mg/2\).
questions.hint_html: The square of the angular-speed multiplier is 2, not √2.

marking_criteria.description_html: Write the radial equation with the horizontal radius.
Check that the orbit is below the rim.

questions.title: Two strings supporting a horizontal orbit
questions.prompt_html:
Two fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) lie on a vertical line with \(A\) above \(B\) and \(AB=6l/5\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is joined to each point by a separate light inextensible string of length \(l\). Both strings are taut as \(P\) moves in a horizontal circle with angular speed \(\omega\).

  1. Find the tension in \(AP\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Equal string lengths put \(P\) halfway between the heights of \(A\) and \(B\). Each vertical separation is \(3l/5\), and the circle radius is \(4l/5\). Thus \[\frac35(T_A-T_B)=mg,\qquad \frac45(T_A+T_B)=m\omega^2\frac{4l}{5}.\] Hence \(T_A-T_B=5mg/3\), while \(T_A+T_B=ml\omega^2\). Adding yields the stated \(T_A\). The assumption that both strings carry positive tension requires \(\omega^2\gt 5g/(3l)\); equality is the zero-tension boundary for the lower string.
questions.hint_html: The two tensions need not be equal: the two strings are separate.

questions.title: A rotating mass at the height of its counterweight
questions.prompt_html:
A light inextensible string of total length \(15a\) passes through a fixed smooth ring \(R\). One end supports a particle \(A\) of mass \(5m\), hanging at rest. The other end is attached to a particle \(B\) of mass \(2m\), which moves in a horizontal circle. The centre of this circle is \(A\), so \(A\) and \(B\) are at the same height. The string is taut.

  1. Find the angular speed of B.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The common tension is \(T=5mg\). If \(\theta\) is the angle of \(RB\) with the downward vertical, vertical balance for \(B\) gives \(T\cos\theta=2mg\), so \(\cos\theta=2/5\). Let \(RB=L\). Equal heights imply \(RA=L\cos\theta=2L/5\). Since \(RA+RB=15a\), \(L=75a/7\). The circle radius is \(L\sin\theta\), so the inward equation is \[T\sin\theta=2m\omega^2L\sin\theta.\] Thus \(\omega^2=5g/(2L)=7g/(30a)\), and the positive square root is required.
questions.hint_html: Use the equal-height condition; the two portions of string do not have equal lengths.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the stationary mass to find tension.

questions.title: A short conical pendulum
questions.prompt_html:
A particle is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(5a\). It moves steadily in a horizontal circle. The string makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical, where \(\tan\theta=3/4\).

  1. Find its angular speed.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The angle has \(\cos\theta=4/5\). For tension \(T\), vertical balance and horizontal circular motion give \[T\cos\theta=mg,\qquad T\sin\theta=m\omega^2(5a\sin\theta).\] Cancel the nonzero \(\sin\theta\), then eliminate \(T\): \(\omega^2=g/(5a\cos\theta)=g/(4a)\).
questions.hint_html: The vertical drop below the point of suspension is 4a.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the actual horizontal radius in the radial equation.

questions.title: Two particles on successive conical strings
questions.prompt_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(2m\) is joined to a fixed point \(O\) by a light string of length \(5a\). A second particle \(Q\) of mass \(m\) is joined to \(P\) by another light inextensible string. Both strings are taut. The particles rotate steadily with the same angular speed about the vertical through \(O\). Their radii are \(3a\) and \(6a\), respectively. At every instant they are on the same side of the axis, in the same vertical half-plane, with \(Q\) below and farther from the axis than \(P\).

  1. Find the tension in OP.

    [3]

  2. Find the common angular speed.

    [3]

  3. Find the angle \(\beta\) that \(PQ\) makes with the downward vertical.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For \(OP\), \(\sin\alpha=3/5\) and \(\cos\alpha=4/5\). The upper string supports the weights of both particles: the vertical components of the force in \(PQ\) cancel when their two vertical equations are added. Hence \(T_1(4/5)=3mg\), giving \(T_1=15mg/4\).

Part (b)

Adding the two horizontal inward equations cancels the internal force from \(PQ\). The total required inward force is \((2m)(3a)\omega^2+m(6a)\omega^2=12ma\omega^2\). Therefore \[\frac{15mg}{4}\frac35=12ma\omega^2,\] which gives \(\omega^2=3g/(16a)\).

Part (c)

For \(Q\) alone, \(T_2\cos\beta=mg\) and \(T_2\sin\beta=m(6a)\omega^2\). Dividing gives \(\tan\beta=6a\omega^2/g=9/8\). The acute angle is selected by the stated geometry.
questions.hint_html: Add the equations of the two particles to remove the force in the lower string.

marking_criteria.description_html: Add radial equations, cancelling the internal force.
Use both masses and their different radii.
Find the angle in the specified geometry.

questions.title: Speed from the geometry of a conical orbit
questions.prompt_html:
A light inextensible string of length \(2a\) joins a particle of mass \(m\) to a fixed point. The particle moves steadily in a horizontal circle. The string makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical, where \(\cos\theta=3/5\).

  1. Find the speed of the particle.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Vertical balance gives \(T(3/5)=mg\), so \(T=5mg/3\). The circle radius is \(2a\sin\theta=8a/5\), and the inward component of tension is \(T(4/5)\). Therefore \[\frac{4mg}{3}=\frac{mv^2}{8a/5},\qquad v^2=\frac{32ag}{15}.\] Taking the positive square root gives the speed.
questions.hint_html: Find the radius of the orbit rather than using the string length directly.

questions.title: A ring above a table and a suspended counterweight
questions.prompt_html:
A light inextensible string of length \(3a\) passes through a fixed smooth ring \(R\) above a smooth horizontal table. One end is attached to a particle \(P\) of mass \(4m\), which moves steadily in a horizontal circle on the table with speed \(\frac45\sqrt{ag}\). The other end supports a particle \(Q\) of mass \(2m\), hanging in equilibrium below \(R\) and above the table. The normal reaction on \(P\) is \(14mg/5\). Let \(\theta\) be the angle of \(RP\) with the downward vertical.

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(RQ\), and check that \(Q\) is above the table.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\theta=3/5\).

(b)

\(RQ=a\), while the ring is \(6a/5\) above the table.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Since \(Q\) is stationary, \(T=2mg\). For \(P\), \(14mg/5+T\cos\theta=4mg\). Hence \(2\cos\theta=6/5\), giving \(\cos\theta=3/5\).

Part (b)

Write \(RP=L\). Its horizontal projection is \(L\sin\theta=4L/5\). The radial equation is \[2mg\frac45=\frac{4m(16ag/25)}{4L/5}.\] This gives \(L=2a\). The remaining string length is \(RQ=3a-2a=a\). The ring height is \(L\cos\theta=6a/5\), which is greater than \(RQ\); therefore \(Q\) is above the table by \(a/5\).
questions.hint_html: The table reaction means the rotating particle is not a free conical pendulum.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check the suspended mass clears the table.

questions.title: A speed from a shared string and a level condition
questions.prompt_html:
A light inextensible string of length \(5a\) passes through a fixed smooth ring. A particle of mass \(4m\) hangs at rest from one end. A particle of mass \(m\) at the other end moves steadily in a horizontal circle. The particles are at the same height. Let \(\theta\) be the angle of the sloping string to the downward vertical.

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [2]

  2. Find the linear speed of the rotating particle.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The tension is \(4mg\). The rotating particle has no vertical acceleration, so \(4mg\cos\theta=mg\), giving \(\cos\theta=1/4\).

Part (b)

If the sloping length is \(L\), the vertical length is \(L/4\). Their sum is \(5a\), so \(L=4a\). Also \(\sin\theta=\sqrt{15}/4\), giving a circle radius \(r=\sqrt{15}a\). The inward force is \(4mg\sin\theta=\sqrt{15}mg\). Hence \[\sqrt{15}mg=\frac{mv^2}{\sqrt{15}a},\] so \(v^2=15ag\).
questions.hint_html: First determine the sloping portion of the string.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the hanging particle to obtain tension.

questions.title: A shared string and a specified angular speed
questions.prompt_html:
A light inextensible string of length \(4a\) passes through a fixed smooth ring \(R\). A particle of mass \(2m\) hangs at rest at distance \(x\) below the ring. A particle of mass \(m\) at the other end moves steadily in a horizontal circle with angular speed \(\sqrt{g/a}\). The sloping portion makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical. No equal-height condition is imposed.

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\) and \(x\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The common tension is \(2mg\). Vertical balance for the rotating particle gives \(2mg\cos\theta=mg\), so \(\cos\theta=1/2\). If the sloping length is \(L\), the radial equation is \(2mg\sin\theta=m\omega^2L\sin\theta\). Since the orbit is nonzero, cancel \(\sin\theta\) to obtain \(2mg=m(g/a)L\). Thus \(L=2a\), and \(x=4a-L=2a\). The rotating particle is only \(L\cos\theta=a\) below the ring. It is not at the same height as the stationary particle.
questions.hint_html: Use the stated angular speed, not an unstated level constraint.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the radial equation with the projected radius.
Deduce x without an unwarranted equal-height condition.

questions.title: Two conical pendulums on one string
questions.prompt_html:
A single light inextensible string passes through two small smooth holes \(C\) and \(D\) in a horizontal table. The part above the table joins the holes. Below \(C\), a particle \(A\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a sloping portion of length \(5a\). Below \(D\), a particle \(B\) of mass \(2m\) is attached to a sloping portion of length \(2a\). The holes are far enough apart that the two motions do not interfere. Each particle moves steadily in its own horizontal circle. The first string makes angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical, and the second makes angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal. The angular speeds are \(\omega\) and \(k\omega\), respectively.

  1. Find \(\tan\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find k.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Because the same light string passes through smooth holes, its tension is common. Vertical balance gives \(T\cos\theta=mg\) for \(A\), and \(T\sin\theta=2mg\) for \(B\). Divide the second equation by the first to obtain \(\tan\theta=2\).

Part (b)

For \(A\), the horizontal radius is \(5a\sin\theta\), so \(T=m(5a)\omega^2\) after cancelling \(\sin\theta\). For \(B\), the radius is \(2a\cos\theta\), giving \(T=(2m)(2a)k^2\omega^2\). Thus \(5=4k^2\). Since angular speeds are positive, \(k=\sqrt5/2\).
questions.hint_html: The two stated angles are measured from different reference directions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the correct radius for A and its radial equation.
Find the correct radius for B and its radial equation.

questions.title: A counterweight that must remain above the table
questions.prompt_html:
A fixed smooth ring is at height \(h\) above a smooth horizontal table. A light inextensible string of total length \(12h/5\) passes through it. A particle of mass \(m\) at one end moves steadily on the table in a horizontal circle; a particle of mass \(3m/4\) at the other end hangs at rest. In one motion the angular speed is \(\omega\), the sloping string angle to the downward vertical is \(\theta\), and the table reaction is \(N\). In a second motion the angular speed is \(\sqrt{3/2}\,\omega\), the angle is \(\alpha\), and the reaction is \(3N/4\).

  1. Show that \(\cos\alpha=\frac32\cos\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(N\) and \(\cos\alpha\).

    [4]

  3. Check that the hanging particle is above the table in both motions.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\alpha=\frac32\cos\theta\).

(b)

\(N=2mg/3\), \(\cos\alpha=2/3\).

(c)

Its distances below the ring are \(3h/20\) and \(9h/10\), both less than \(h\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The tension is fixed at \(3mg/4\). If the sloping length is \(L\), the radial equation gives \(T=m\omega^2L\). Since \(L\cos\theta=h\), it follows that \(\cos\theta=mh\omega^2/T\). Replacing \(\omega^2\) by \(3\omega^2/2\) gives the claimed relation.

Part (b)

Let \(c=\cos\theta\). Vertical balances are \[N=mg-\frac34mgc,\qquad \frac34N=mg-\frac34mg\left(\frac32c\right).\] Substitution gives \(3/4-9c/16=1-9c/8\), hence \(c=4/9\). Therefore \(\cos\alpha=2/3\), and \(N=mg(1-1/3)=2mg/3\). Both normal reactions are positive.

Part (c)

The sloping lengths are \(h/(4/9)=9h/4\) and \(h/(2/3)=3h/2\). Subtracting from \(12h/5\) gives \(3h/20\) and \(9h/10\). Both are positive and less than \(h\), so the hanging particle remains clear of the table in both cases.
questions.hint_html: The total length is needed for the clearance check, not for the force ratio.

marking_criteria.description_html: Eliminate the radius to relate length and angular speed.
Find the two vertical portions of string.
Check both lie strictly between zero and h.

questions.title: A raised elastic tether on a rough turntable
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\ \mathrm{kg}\) remains at a distance \(1.2\ \mathrm m\) from the axis of a rough horizontal rotating disc. It is attached to a fixed point \(A\) on the axis above the disc by a light elastic string of natural length \(1.6\ \mathrm m\) and modulus \(40\ \mathrm N\). In the steady motion the tension is \(10\ \mathrm N\). The coefficient of friction is \(1/3\). Let \(\alpha\) be the angle between the string and the vertical. Take \(g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find \(\sin\alpha\) and the normal reaction of the disc.

    [3]

  2. At the greatest possible steady rotation rate the particle is about to slip radially outwards. Find this rate in revolutions per minute.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Hooke’s law gives extension \(e=T l/\lambda=10(1.6)/40=0.4\ \mathrm m\). The string length is \(2\ \mathrm m\), so \(\sin\alpha=1.2/2=3/5\) and \(\cos\alpha=4/5\). Vertical balance is \(N+10(4/5)=20\), giving \(N=12\ \mathrm N\).

Part (b)

Impending outward slip means friction acts inwards. Its limiting magnitude is \(\mu N=4\ \mathrm N\); the inward component of the string tension is \(10(3/5)=6\ \mathrm N\). Therefore \[6+4=2(1.2)\omega^2,\qquad \omega^2=\frac{25}{6}.\] There are \(60\omega/(2\pi)\) revolutions per minute, giving \(150/(\pi\sqrt6)\). The positive normal reaction found in (a) confirms that contact with the disc is possible.
questions.hint_html: The upward component of the tension reduces the normal reaction, and therefore reduces the available friction.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use Hooke’s law and the extended length.
Choose inward friction at the outward threshold.
Find angular speed from all inward forces.

questions.title: Extension at a prescribed angular speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\ \mathrm{kg}\) moves on a smooth horizontal table, attached to a fixed point on the table by a light elastic string of natural length \(1\ \mathrm m\) and modulus \(60\ \mathrm N\). Its constant angular speed is \(3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find the extension of the string.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write the extension as \(e\ \mathrm m\). Hooke’s law gives \(T=60e\), and the circle radius is \(1+e\). Thus \[60e=2(1+e)3^2.\] So \(42e=18\), yielding \(e=3/7\ \mathrm m\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html: Use the stretched length as the radius.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the extended length in the radial equation.

questions.title: One elastic string through a table
questions.prompt_html:
A light elastic string has natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\). It passes through a small smooth hole \(H\) in a smooth horizontal table. A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to one end and moves in a horizontal circle about \(H\), with speed \(\sqrt{3ga/2}\). A particle \(Q\) of mass \(km\) hangs in equilibrium from the other end, with \(HQ=a/2\).

  1. Find the total extension of the string.

    [4]

  2. Find k.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write the total extension as \(za\). The common tension is \(3mgz\). The horizontal radius is the total stretched length less the vertical portion: \[r=a(1+z)-a/2=a(z+1/2).\] The radial equation for \(P\) is \[3mgz=\frac{m(3ga/2)}{a(z+1/2)}.\] This reduces to \(2z^2+z-1=0=(2z-1)(z+1)\). Extension must be positive, so \(z=1/2\), not \(-1\).

Part (b)

The hanging particle is at rest, so \(kmg=T=3mg(1/2)\). Hence \(k=3/2\). With this value the total length is \(3a/2\), the horizontal radius is \(a\), and the vertical portion is \(a/2\), as required.
questions.hint_html: Hooke’s law uses the extension of the whole string, not just the horizontal portion.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the horizontal radius from total length.

questions.title: Comparing two masses on the same elastic string
questions.prompt_html:
A light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(\lambda mg\) is fixed at one end on a smooth horizontal table. A particle of mass \(m\), attached to the other end, moves steadily in a circle of radius \(x\) with speed \(v\). In a separate experiment a particle of mass \(3m\) is attached to the same string and moves steadily with speed \(v/3\) in a circle of radius \(2x/3\). Both motions have positive tension.

  1. Find \(x\) in terms of \(a\).

    [5]

  2. Given that \(v=\sqrt{18ag}\), find \(\lambda\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For the first experiment, \[\frac{\lambda mg(x-a)}{a}=\frac{mv^2}{x}.\] For the second, the required force is \(3m(v/3)^2/(2x/3)=mv^2/(2x)\). Dividing the second elastic-force equation by the first gives \[\frac{2x/3-a}{x-a}=\frac12.\] Thus \(4x/3-2a=x-a\), so \(x=3a\). The radii are \(3a\) and \(2a\), both greater than the natural length; both assumed tensions are therefore positive.

Part (b)

Substitute \(x=3a\) into the first equation: \(2\lambda mg=m(18ag)/(3a)=6mg\). Hence \(\lambda=3\).
questions.hint_html: Compare the two tensions by dividing the radial equations.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the second radial equation with the changed mass and speed.

questions.title: An elastic pendulum with a specified vertical drop
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(kmg\). It moves steadily in a horizontal circle whose centre is \(8a\) vertically below \(O\). Its speed is \(\frac32\sqrt{2ag}\).

  1. Find the extension of the string.

    [4]

  2. Find k.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let the horizontal circle radius be \(r\), the string length be \(L\), and its angle to the downward vertical be \(\theta\). Dividing the horizontal and vertical force equations gives \[\tan\theta=\frac{v^2}{rg}.\] Geometry gives \(\tan\theta=r/(8a)\). Hence \(r^2=8av^2/g=36a^2\), so \(r=6a\). Thus \(L=\sqrt{(6a)^2+(8a)^2}=10a\). The extension is \(10a-6a=4a\).

Part (b)

The string angle has \(\cos\theta=8/10=4/5\). Vertical equilibrium therefore gives \(T=5mg/4\). Hooke’s law gives \[T=\frac{kmg(4a)}{6a}=\frac23kmg.\] Thus \(2k/3=5/4\), and \(k=15/8\). The tension is positive, consistent with the extension found in (a).
questions.hint_html: The ratio of the force equations gives the horizontal radius before Hooke’s law is needed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the ratio of horizontal and vertical equations.
Use Hooke’s law with the natural length.

questions.title: An elastic string at a prescribed speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a point on a smooth horizontal plane by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(5mg\). It moves steadily in a horizontal circle with speed \(\sqrt{15ag/4}\).

  1. Find the extension of the string.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put the extension equal to \(za\), where \(z\gt 0\). The radius is \(a(1+z)\) and the tension is \(5mgz\). Thus \[5mgz=\frac{m(15ag/4)}{a(1+z)},\qquad 4z^2+4z-3=0.\] The roots are \(z=1/2\) and \(z=-3/2\). The latter would give a negative radius and is impossible. Therefore the extension is \(a/2\).
questions.hint_html: The radius is the natural length plus the extension.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use stretched length in the radial equation.

questions.title: Finding the angle after finding the elastic length
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light elastic string of natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(6mg\). It moves steadily in a horizontal circle with angular speed \(\sqrt{g/a}\). The stretched string length is \(2a(1+k)\), and its angle to the downward vertical is \(\theta\).

  1. Find k.

    [3]

  2. Find \(\cos\theta\), and verify that the orbit is non-degenerate.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The extension is \(2ak\), so Hooke’s law gives \(T=6mgk\). The radial equation, after cancelling \(\sin\theta\ne0\), gives \(T=m\omega^2L=2mg(1+k)\). Therefore \(6k=2(1+k)\), and \(k=1/2\).

Part (b)

The tension is \(T=3mg\), and vertical balance gives \(3mg\cos\theta=mg\), so \(\cos\theta=1/3\). The length is \(3a\), so the horizontal radius is \(3a\sqrt{1-1/9}=2\sqrt2a\gt 0\). The extension is also positive, as assumed.
questions.hint_html: In the radial equation the sine cancels, but only for a nonzero orbit.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the radial equation and stretched length.
Check a positive horizontal radius and extension.

questions.title: Reaching an upper point of a spherical surface
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves in a vertical plane on the smooth inside of a fixed spherical shell of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\). In that plane use coordinates relative to \(O\), with horizontal \(x\) and upward \(y\). It is projected vertically downwards from \(A=(-a,0)\) with speed \(u\), passes through the lowest point and ascends on the right. Let \(B\) be the point on this ascent with \(y=ka\), where \(0\lt k\lt 1\).

  1. In one experiment \(u^2=8ag/5\), and the reaction at B is one quarter of the reaction at A. Find k.

    [4]

  2. For this value of k, find the least launch speed that allows the particle to reach B without losing contact before B.

    [3]

  3. At this least launch speed the particle leaves the surface at B. Find its greatest height above O during the ensuing free flight.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Energy between \(A\) and \(B\) gives \(v_B^2=u^2-2gka\). At \(A\), gravity has no radial component, so \(N_A=mu^2/a\). At \(B\), the inward component of weight is \(mgk\), giving \[N_B=\frac{mv_B^2}{a}-mgk=\frac{mu^2}{a}-3mgk.\] Thus \(8/5-3k=(1/4)(8/5)\), so \(k=2/5\).

Part (b)

While contact is maintained, \(N/(mg)=u^2/(ag)-3y/a\). On the upper ascent this is smallest at \(B\), so nonnegative reaction up to \(B\) requires \(u^2/(ag)\ge3k=6/5\). Equality gives the least speed. At \(B\), \(v_B^2=agk=2ag/5\gt 0\). Merely requiring \(v_B^2\ge0\) would give too small a launch speed.

Part (c)

At release, \(\cos\theta=k=2/5\), \(v_B^2=2ag/5\), and the upward component of velocity is \(v_B\sin\theta\). Its square is \((2ag/5)(21/25)=42ag/125\). The additional rise is this quantity divided by \(2g\), namely \(21a/125\). Add the release height \(2a/5\) to get \(71a/125\). The apex occurs before recontact with the shell.
questions.hint_html: Use energy and the nonnegative normal reaction together. After release, switch to projectile equations.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the reactions at A and B with correct radial weight.
Apply nonnegative reaction, not only nonnegative speed.

questions.title: Slackness followed by an upward free flight
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at the point \((a,0)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\), and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{9ag/5}\). It passes through the lowest point and subsequently rises on the left.

  1. Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at which the string first becomes slack.

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest height above O during the free flight immediately following slackening.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(y=ca\) on the ascending upper part of the circle. Energy from the initial horizontal position gives \(v^2/(ag)=9/5-2c\). Taking inward force as positive, \[T+mgc=\frac{mv^2}{a},\qquad \frac{T}{mg}=\frac95-3c.\] Thus the first zero tension occurs at \(c=3/5\). The speed there satisfies \(v^2=3ag/5\gt 0\), so this is loss of the circular constraint rather than a turning point.

Part (b)

At release the height is \(3a/5\), and \(\sin\theta=4/5\). The upward tangential velocity component has magnitude \(v_y=(4/5)\sqrt{3ag/5}\). Its square is \(48ag/125\). During free flight the additional rise is \(v_y^2/(2g)=24a/125\). Therefore the greatest height is \[\frac35a+\frac{24}{125}a=\frac{99}{125}a.\] This apex occurs while the string is slack. In dimensionless time \(\tau=t\sqrt{g/a}\), recontact with the original circle would occur at \(4\sin\theta\sqrt{\cos\theta}\), whereas the apex is at only \(\sin\theta\sqrt{\cos\theta}\).
questions.hint_html: Use the vertical component of the release velocity, not the whole speed, to find the extra rise.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify that the apex is in the unconstrained phase.

questions.title: Motion after a tension-triggered break
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is joined to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at \((a,0)\), using horizontal and upward axes through \(O\), and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{ag/2}\). The string breaks when its tension first reaches \(2mg\). Thereafter the particle moves freely under gravity.

  1. Find the cosine of the angle to the downward vertical at breaking, and the speed at that instant.

    [4]

  2. Find the time from breaking until the particle is vertically below O.

    [4]

  3. Find the distance from O at this time.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

On the initial descent write the downward vertical cosine as \(c\), so the height is \(-ac\). Energy gives \(v^2=ag(1/2+2c)\). The inward equation is \(T-mgc=mv^2/a\), giving \(T/(mg)=1/2+3c\). Setting this to 2 gives \(c=1/2\), which occurs before the bottom. The speed squared is then \(3ag/2\).

Part (b)

At breaking the position is \((\sqrt3a/2,-a/2)\). Since motion is downwards and leftwards along the tangent, the velocity components are \(-v/2\) and \(-\sqrt3v/2\). Horizontal motion then gives \[0=\frac{\sqrt3a}{2}-\frac v2t,\qquad t=\frac{\sqrt3a}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2a}{g}}.\] The positive time is unique because the horizontal velocity is a negative constant.

Part (c)

The vertical position is \[y=-\frac a2-\frac{\sqrt3v}{2}t-\frac12gt^2.\] Using \(vt=\sqrt3a\) and \(gt^2=2a\), this becomes \(y=-a/2-3a/2-a=-3a\). The horizontal coordinate is zero, so the distance from \(O\) is \(3a\), not the signed coordinate \(-3a\).
questions.hint_html: At breaking the tangent points down and towards the vertical axis.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain tension as a function of the downward cosine.
Find the release speed and locate the event.
Resolve the release velocity with correct signs.
Convert the signed height to a distance.

questions.title: An impact angle after leaving a sphere
questions.prompt_html:
A smooth solid sphere of radius \(a\) is fixed with its lowest point on horizontal ground. A small particle is projected horizontally from its highest point with speed \(u\), initially following the outer surface. After leaving the sphere it moves freely and strikes the ground with speed \(\sqrt{11}\,u\). Let \(\beta\) be the acute angle its velocity makes below the horizontal at impact.

  1. Find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [2]

  2. Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at loss of contact.

    [3]

  3. Find \(\beta\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The total fall from the top to the ground is \(2a\). Energy is conserved both on the smooth surface and during flight, giving \(11u^2=u^2+4ag\). Hence \(u^2=2ag/5\).

Part (b)

Write \(c=\cos\theta\). At release, \(N=0\) and the inward component of weight gives \(v^2=agc\). Energy from the top gives \(v^2=u^2+2ag(1-c)\). Hence \(3c=2+2/5=12/5\), so \(c=4/5\). The initial reaction is \(mg-mu^2/a=3mg/5\gt 0\), so the initial contact assumption holds.

Part (c)

At release, the horizontal component of the tangential velocity is \(v\cos\theta\). Its square is \(agc^3=64ag/125\). This component is unchanged in flight. The impact speed squared is \(11u^2=22ag/5\), so \[\cos^2\beta=\frac{64ag/125}{22ag/5}=\frac{32}{275}.\] Select the acute angle, since the impact velocity is downwards and forwards.
questions.hint_html: Use energy for the final speed, but use the unchanged horizontal component for its direction.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use total energy from top to ground.
Use zero reaction on the exterior surface.
Find the impact angle in the correct quadrant.

questions.title: Crossing the vertical axis after leaving a cylinder
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves on the smooth inside of a fixed circular cylinder of radius \(a\), in a vertical cross-section with centre \(O\). Starting at \((-a,0)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\), it is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{12ag/5}\). It passes through the lowest point and ascends on the right before losing contact.

  1. Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at loss of contact.

    [3]

  2. Find the height above O when the particle first crosses the vertical through O after release, and state whether it is then rising or falling.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At a height \(ac\), energy gives \(v^2/(ag)=12/5-2c\). The reaction is \(N/(mg)=12/5-3c\). Setting \(N=0\) gives \(c=4/5\), with positive release speed \(v=\sqrt{4ag/5}\).

Part (b)

At release, \((x,y)=(3a/5,4a/5)\). The velocity points up and left, with components \(-4v/5\) and \(3v/5\). Horizontal motion gives elapsed time \[t=\frac{3a}{4v}=\frac{3\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{\frac ag}.\] The vertical position is \(y=4a/5+(3v/5)t-gt^2/2\). Here \((3v/5)t=9a/20\) and \(gt^2/2=45a/128\), so \(y=115a/128\). At this time the vertical velocity is \((6\sqrt5/25-3\sqrt5/8)\sqrt{ag}=-27\sqrt5\sqrt{ag}/200\lt 0\). The particle is falling. The axis-crossing point is inside the cylinder; the first positive recontact time is \((24\sqrt5/25)\sqrt{a/g}\), which is later.
questions.hint_html: Write separate horizontal and vertical equations from the release point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Determine the sign of the vertical velocity and valid flight phase.

questions.title: Time of flight after leaving the outside of a sphere
questions.prompt_html:
A fixed smooth solid sphere of radius \(a\) rests on horizontal ground. A particle of mass \(m\) is launched horizontally from the top with speed \(u\). It follows the outer surface and leaves it where the radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical. After leaving, it moves freely under gravity.

  1. Show that \(\cos\theta=(u^2+2ag)/(3ag)\).

    [3]

  2. Given that \(\cos\theta=3/4\), find the vertical velocity just before ground impact.

    [3]

  3. Find the elapsed time between leaving the sphere and ground impact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\theta=(u^2+2ag)/(3ag)\).

(b)

\(\displaystyle-\frac{7\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{ag}\), taking upwards as positive.

(c)

\(\displaystyle t=\frac{7\sqrt5-\sqrt{21}}8\sqrt{\frac ag}\approx1.38\sqrt{\frac ag}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At angle \(\theta\), energy gives \(v^2=u^2+2ag(1-\cos\theta)\). On the outside, the normal force acts outwards, so \(mg\cos\theta-N=mv^2/a\). At loss of contact \(N=0\); substitute \(v^2=ag\cos\theta\) into energy and rearrange to obtain the stated result.

Part (b)

The release speed squared is \(3ag/4\), and \(\sin^2\theta=7/16\). The release vertical velocity is downward, with square \(21ag/64\). The release height above the ground is \(a(1+3/4)=7a/4\). Thus the impact vertical speed squared is \(21ag/64+2g(7a/4)=245ag/64\). The signed velocity is \(-7\sqrt5\sqrt{ag}/8\).

Part (c)

The vertical release velocity is \(-\sqrt{21}\sqrt{ag}/8\). Since \(v_y=v_{y0}-gt\), \[-\frac{7\sqrt5}{8}\sqrt{ag}=-\frac{\sqrt{21}}8\sqrt{ag}-gt.\] Therefore \(t=(7\sqrt5-\sqrt{21})\sqrt{a/g}/8\). It is positive. Part (a) also gives \(u^2=ag/4\lt ag\), so initial contact at the top is physically possible.
questions.hint_html: Use downward velocity signs consistently; the release point is above the centre, not above ground by only a cosθ.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the fall from the release height.
Use vertical velocity change during free flight.
Give the requested exact and approximate forms.

questions.title: A deliberate release on the lower ascending arc
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at a horizontal level with \(O\) and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{3ag/5}\). After passing the bottom it reaches a point \(Q\) on the lower ascending arc, where the string makes acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical. At \(Q\), its speed is \(\sqrt{kag}\) and its tension is \(12mg/5\). It is then deliberately detached from the string.

  1. Find \(k\) and \(\cos\theta\).

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest height above the lowest point reached during the subsequent free flight.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\). The point \(Q\) is \(ac\) below the starting level, so energy gives \(k=3/5+2c\). The radial equation at the lower point is \(12mg/5-mgc=mkg\), or \(k+c=12/5\). Combining gives \(3/5+3c=12/5\), so \(c=3/5\) and \(k=9/5\).

Part (b)

At release, \(Q\) is \(a(1-3/5)=2a/5\) above the lowest point. Its upward tangential component is \(v\sin\theta\), with square \((9ag/5)(16/25)=144ag/125\). The additional rise is \(72a/125\). Therefore the greatest height above the lowest point is \[\frac25a+\frac{72}{125}a=\frac{122}{125}a.\] This is slightly below the horizontal level through \(O\). The release is imposed deliberately; it does not occur because the tension is zero.
questions.hint_html: The particle is ascending even though it is still below the centre.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the release height above the lowest point.
Add heights with the correct reference level.

questions.title: Locating the next contact after release
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves on the smooth inner surface of a fixed circular cylinder of radius \(a\), in a vertical cross-section with centre \(O\). It is projected to the right from the lowest point with speed \(\sqrt{19ag/5}\). After losing contact on the upper right, it moves freely until it next meets the cylinder. Use horizontal and upward coordinates relative to \(O\).

  1. Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at loss of contact.

    [3]

  2. Find the next contact point and the elapsed time from release to that contact.

    [5]

  3. Explain why this is the first contact after release.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The bottom-to-point rise is \(a(1+c)\), with \(c\) the upward cosine. Thus \(v^2/(ag)=19/5-2(1+c)=9/5-2c\). At zero reaction \(v^2=agc\), giving \(c=3/5\). The release coordinates are \((4a/5,3a/5)\).

Part (b)

At release \(v=\sqrt{3ag/5}\), directed up and left. Write \(X=x/a\), \(Y=y/a\) and \(\tau=t\sqrt{g/a}\). The free-flight equations are \[X=\frac45-\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{25}\tau,\qquad Y=\frac35+\frac{4\sqrt{15}}{25}\tau-\frac12\tau^2.\] Substitute these into the cylinder equation \(X^2+Y^2=1\). Expansion and factorisation give \[X^2+Y^2-1=\tau^3\left(\frac{\tau}{4}-\frac{4\sqrt{15}}{25}\right).\] The positive root is \(\tau=16\sqrt{15}/25\). Substitution gives \(X=-44/125\), \(Y=-117/125\). Restore dimensions for the time and coordinates.

Part (c)

In the factorisation above, \(\tau^3\gt 0\) for positive time and the bracket is negative until the stated positive root. Hence the whole preceding flight lies strictly inside the circle. There is no earlier positive intersection. Also \(44^2+117^2=125^2\), confirming the final point lies on the surface.
questions.hint_html: After release solve for the next intersection with the entire circle; do not assume it is the bottom.

marking_criteria.description_html: Resolve the release velocity and write flight equations.
Substitute into the circle equation and factor correctly.
Use the sign of the factored circle expression.
Exclude all earlier contacts and verify the endpoint.

questions.title: Contact along an arc joining opposite points
questions.prompt_html:
In a vertical section of a fixed smooth spherical shell of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\), let \(A=(-4a/5,-3a/5)\), \(C=(0,-a)\) and \(B=(4a/5,3a/5)\). A particle of mass \(m\) is projected tangentially from \(A\), initially moving towards \(C\), with speed \(u\). The normal reactions at \(A\) and \(C\) are in the ratio \(11:15\).

  1. Find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [4]

  2. Determine whether the particle reaches B while remaining in contact with the surface.

    [5]

  3. Find the greatest reaction before contact is lost and the speed at loss of contact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=27ag/10\).

(b)

No. Contact is lost first at height \(a/2\) above \(O\).

(c)

\(N_{\max}=9mg/2\), \(v_{\rm loss}=\sqrt{ag/2}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The fall from \(A\) to \(C\) is \(2a/5\), so \(v_C^2=u^2+4ag/5\). The inward component of weight at \(A\) is \(-3mg/5\), hence \(N_A=mu^2/a+3mg/5\). At the bottom, \(N_C=mv_C^2/a+mg=mu^2/a+9mg/5\). Writing \(q=u^2/(ag)\), the ratio gives \(15(q+3/5)=11(q+9/5)\). Thus \(4q=54/5\), and \(q=27/10\).

Part (b)

For any point at height \(y=ca\), energy gives \[\frac{v^2}{ag}=\frac{27}{10}+2\left(-\frac35-c\right)=\frac32-2c.\] The inward radial equation gives \(N/(mg)=3/2-3c\). The first zero on the upper ascent is at \(c=1/2\), before the particle reaches the height \(3a/5\) of \(B\). At that zero the speed squared is \(ag/2\gt 0\). At \(B\), energy alone would predict \(v_B^2=3ag/10\gt 0\), but the contact formula would require \(N_B=-3mg/10\). An inner surface cannot pull the particle outwards, so this is not a physically possible continuation in contact.

Part (c)

The expression \(N/(mg)=3/2-3c\) is greatest at the lowest point \(c=-1\), which lies on the actual route. Hence \(N_{\max}=9mg/2\). At loss of contact \(c=1/2\), so \(v^2/(ag)=3/2-1=1/2\), giving \(v=\sqrt{ag/2}\).
questions.hint_html: An inner surface requires a nonnegative inward reaction. Check it before using a later point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the speed as a function of height.
Obtain the reaction as a function of height.
Check positive speed at loss of contact.
Reject contact at B despite the positive energy-only speed.
Locate the maximum reaction on the actual path.

questions.title: A three-quarter turn before slackening
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is joined to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially it is at \(A=(4a/5,3a/5)\), relative to horizontal and upward axes through \(O\). It is projected tangentially in the clockwise, initially downward, direction with speed \(u\). The string first becomes slack after the radius has turned clockwise through \(270^\circ\).

  1. Find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [5]

  2. Find the greatest tension before slackening.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

A clockwise rotation through \(270^\circ\) is equivalent geometrically to an anticlockwise rotation through \(90^\circ\), so the release point is \(B=(-3a/5,4a/5)\). The rise from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(a/5\). Hence \(v_B^2=u^2-2ag/5\). At \(B\), zero tension gives \(v_B^2/a=g(4/5)\). Therefore \(u^2-2ag/5=4ag/5\), giving \(u^2=6ag/5\). The initial tension is \(mg(6/5-3/5)=3mg/5\gt 0\).

Part (b)

At a general height \(y=ca\), conservation of energy gives \(v^2/(ag)=6/5+2(3/5-c)=12/5-2c\). Thus \(T/(mg)=12/5-3c\). Its maximum on the route occurs at the bottom \(c=-1\), giving \(T_{\max}=27mg/5\). On the route from \(A\) downwards and then upwards to \(B\), \(c\le4/5\), with equality first at \(B\), so no earlier slackening is hidden.
questions.hint_html: Locate the endpoint of the 270° turn before writing the energy equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Locate the release point after the stated rotation.
Obtain u squared and check initial tautness.
Find the speed as a function of height.
Obtain tension as a function of height.
Locate the actual lowest point of the route.
Find the maximum and exclude earlier slackening.

questions.title: Two experiments with the same launch speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves on the smooth inner surface of a spherical shell of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\), in one vertical plane. In the first experiment it starts at height \(-a/4\) relative to \(O\), is projected tangentially downwards with speed \(u\), passes the bottom, and loses contact on the opposite ascent at upward radius-angle \(\beta\). In a second experiment it starts at the lowest point with the same speed \(u\), and loses contact at upward radius-angle \(2\beta\). Both loss points are in the upper half of the circle, and \(0\lt \beta\lt \pi/4\).

  1. Show that the first experiment gives \(u^2=ag(\frac12+3\cos\beta)\).

    [5]

  2. Find \(\cos\beta\), rejecting inadmissible roots.

    [5]

  3. Find the reaction at the initial point in the first experiment.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(c=\cos\beta\). The release height is \(ac\), so the gain in height from the first start is \(a(c+1/4)\). At release the normal force is zero, and the radial equation gives \(v^2=agc\). Energy gives \(u^2=v^2+2ag(c+1/4)\). Substitute \(v^2=agc\) to obtain \(u^2=ag(1/2+3c)\). The release speed is positive because \(c\gt 0\).

Part (b)

In the second experiment the height gained is \(a(1+\cos2\beta)\), and the release speed squared is \(ag\cos2\beta\). Hence \(u^2/(ag)=2+3\cos2\beta=6c^2-1\). Equating with (a) gives \(1/2+3c=6c^2-1\), or \(4c^2-2c-1=0\). Thus \(c=(1\pm\sqrt5)/4\). The negative root is impossible; the positive root is between \(\sqrt2/2\) and 1, as required by \(0\lt \beta\lt \pi/4\). Its double-angle cosine is \((\sqrt5-1)/4\gt 0\), so both release points are indeed above the centre.

Part (c)

From (a), \(u^2/(ag)=(5+3\sqrt5)/4\). At the initial point the inward component of gravity is \(-mg/4\), so \[R-\frac14mg=\frac{mu^2}{a}.\] Consequently \(R/(mg)=(5+3\sqrt5)/4+1/4=(6+3\sqrt5)/4\). This is positive, and the reaction stays positive down to the bottom and up to the first stated release point.
questions.hint_html: Use the same u in both experiments, but different initial heights.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply energy from the first starting point.
Check the stated angular interval and upper-half condition.
Use the signed radial component of gravity.

questions.title: An inverse problem for a slack-string event
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\), joined to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\), is projected horizontally from the lowest point with speed \(u\). Its tension there is \(T_0\). At a later point on the upper ascent, the radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical and the tension is \(S\).

  1. Show that \(S=T_0-3mg(1+\cos\theta)\).

    [4]

  2. The string first becomes slack when \(\cos\theta=3/4\). Find \(u\) and \(T_0\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the lowest point \(T_0=mu^2/a+mg\). The rise to the later point is \(a(1+\cos\theta)\), so \(v^2=u^2-2ag(1+\cos\theta)\). Its radial equation is \(S+mg\cos\theta=mv^2/a\). Substitute the energy relation and then eliminate \(mu^2/a=T_0-mg\), obtaining \[S=T_0-3mg-3mg\cos\theta.\]

Part (b)

At slackening \(S=0\), so part (a) gives \(T_0=3mg(1+3/4)=21mg/4\). The bottom equation then gives \(u^2/a=(21/4-1)g=17g/4\), hence \(u=\sqrt{17ag}/2\). The release speed squared is \(3ag/4\gt 0\), and the tension decreases to its first zero on the ascent.
questions.hint_html: Use the release condition to work backwards to the bottom.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the zero-tension event to find T0.
Use the bottom radial equation for u.
Take the positive speed and check the release is feasible.

questions.title: A right-angle separation with a known release speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). At the initial point \(A\), to the right and below \(O\), the radius makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical. It is projected tangentially anticlockwise and upwards. The string first becomes slack at \(B\), after the radius has turned through \(90^\circ\). The speed at \(B\) is \(\sqrt{5ag/13}\).

  1. Find \(\sin\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find the initial tension.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial coordinates are \((a\sin\theta,-a\cos\theta)\). After a quarter turn, \(B=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta)\), so the upward radius-cosine there is \(\sin\theta\). With zero tension, \[mg\sin\theta=\frac{m(5ag/13)}a,\] giving \(\sin\theta=5/13\). The acute-angle condition then gives \(\cos\theta=12/13\).

Part (b)

The rise from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(a(5/13+12/13)=17a/13\). Energy gives \[u^2=\frac5{13}ag+\frac{34}{13}ag=3ag.\] At \(A\), \(T_A-mg\cos\theta=mu^2/a\). Thus \(T_A=mg(3+12/13)=51mg/13\). Along the ascent to \(B\), tension decreases with height and reaches its first zero at the given upper point.
questions.hint_html: The upward cosine at B is the sine of the original downward angle.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply zero tension with the correct weight component.

questions.title: An upper-half slackening point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at an angle \(\alpha\) to the downward vertical, with \(\cos\alpha=3/5\), and is projected tangentially upwards with speed \(\sqrt{16ag/5}\).

  1. Find the cosine of the angle the string makes with the upward vertical when it first becomes slack.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The starting height is \(-3a/5\). At an upper point with upward cosine \(c\), energy gives \[\frac{v^2}{ag}=\frac{16}{5}-2\left(c+\frac35\right)=2-2c.\] At zero tension \(v^2=agc\), so \(2-2c=c\). Thus \(c=2/3\). It is in the upper half and gives a positive release speed squared \(2ag/3\); earlier tension is positive.
questions.hint_html: Use the increase in height from the lower starting position.

questions.title: A boundary case for a vertical circle
questions.prompt_html:
A particle is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially the string makes an acute angle \(\alpha\) to the downward vertical, with \(\cos\alpha=3/8\). The particle is projected tangentially upwards with speed \(\sqrt{15ag/4}\).

  1. Determine whether it turns back before reaching the top, loses the circular constraint before the top, or reaches the top in the limiting complete-circle case. Justify your answer.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

It reaches the top in the limiting complete-circle case, with \(v_{\rm top}=\sqrt{ag}\) and zero tension only at that instant.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial height is \(-3a/8\), so the rise to the top is \(11a/8\). Energy gives \(v_{\rm top}^2=15ag/4-11ag/4=ag\). The energy constant is \(K=15/4-2(3/8)=3\). At a general height \(y=ca\), the squared speed is \(ag(3-2c)\), which is positive throughout the circle. The tension is \(3mg(1-c)\), nonnegative throughout and zero only at the top \(c=1\). Consequently there is neither a turning point nor an earlier slack phase; this is the limiting complete-circle solution.
questions.hint_html: Test both speed and tension, including points just before the top.

marking_criteria.description_html: Write speed squared over the whole circle.
Write the tension over the whole circle.

questions.title: Choosing the launch speed for a prescribed loss point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle joined to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\) starts on the lower half of a vertical circle, with its radius at angle \(\alpha\) to the downward vertical and \(\cos\alpha=2/5\). It is launched tangentially upwards with speed \(u\). The string is to become slack for the first time at an upper point whose radius has cosine \(3/5\) to the upward vertical.

  1. Find \(u\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the required loss point, zero tension gives \(v^2=3ag/5\). Its height is \(3a/5\), while the initial height is \(-2a/5\), so the rise is \(a\). Energy therefore gives \(u^2=3ag/5+2ag=13ag/5\). The resulting tension decreases continuously on the ascent to its first zero, and the release speed is positive.
questions.hint_html: Start with the known loss-point geometry and work backwards.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use zero tension to obtain the release speed.
Find the rise from the stated starting point.
Check the first-loss condition and take the positive root.

questions.title: A release speed given as a fraction of the launch speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially it is below and to the right of \(O\), with its radius making acute angle \(\theta\) to the downward vertical. It is projected tangentially anticlockwise upwards with speed \(u\). After a quarter turn, at \(B\), the string first becomes slack. Its speed at \(B\) is \(u/\sqrt6\).

  1. Find \(\tan\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Find the initial tension.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write \(s=\sin\theta\) and \(c=\cos\theta\). The quarter-turn point has height \(as\), and the starting height is \(-ac\). At release the zero-tension condition is \[\frac{u^2}{6a}=gs,\qquad u^2=6ags.\] Energy between the two points gives \(u^2-u^2/6=2ag(s+c)\). Substitution yields \(5s=2s+2c\), so \(3s=2c\) and \(\tan\theta=2/3\).

Part (b)

The acute angle has \(s=2/\sqrt{13}\), \(c=3/\sqrt{13}\). Thus \(u^2=12ag/\sqrt{13}\). At the lower starting point, \(T_A-mgc=mu^2/a\), giving \(T_A=(12+3)mg/\sqrt{13}=15mg/\sqrt{13}\). The initial tension is positive and falls to zero only at the stated release height.
questions.hint_html: Use the square of the speed ratio: the release kinetic energy is one sixth of the initial value.

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate the quarter-turn geometry to the two heights.
Apply energy using the squared speed ratio.
Find the sine and cosine of the acute angle.
Use the initial radial equation for tension.

questions.title: Leaving the exterior of a sphere from a non-top start
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) starts on the smooth outer surface of a fixed sphere of radius \(a\). The starting radius makes acute angle \(\alpha\) with the upward vertical, where \(\cos\alpha=3/4\). It is projected tangentially downwards along a vertical great circle with speed \(\frac12\sqrt{ag}\). It leaves the sphere where the radius makes angle \(\beta\) to the upward vertical.

  1. Find \(\cos\beta\).

    [3]

  2. Check that the particle initially remains in contact and that the computed point is its first loss point.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\beta=7/12\).

(b)

\(N_A=mg/2\gt 0\); the reaction decreases to its first zero at \(\cos\beta=7/12\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Energy from the starting point to a point with upward cosine \(c\) gives \(v^2/(ag)=1/4+2(3/4-c)=7/4-2c\). On the exterior surface, \(mgc-N=mv^2/a\). At loss of contact \(N=0\), so \(c=7/4-2c\), giving \(c=7/12\).

Part (b)

Initially \(N_A=mg(3/4-1/4)=mg/2\gt 0\). In general \(N/(mg)=3c-7/4\). During the descent \(c\) decreases from \(3/4\), so this expression stays positive until its unique first zero at \(7/12\). The release speed squared is \(7ag/12\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html: For an exterior surface the normal force points away from the centre.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check positive reaction at the launch point.
Use monotonicity along the descent to verify first loss.

questions.title: Opposite points and a tension ratio
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Points \(A\) and \(B\) are opposite ends of a diameter of the vertical circle. Point \(A\) is above the centre and \(OA\) makes an acute angle \(\alpha\) with the upward vertical. At \(A\) the speed is \(\sqrt{3ag}\). The tension at \(B\) is twice that at \(A\).

  1. Find \(\cos\alpha\).

    [4]

  2. Find the tension at B.

    [2]

  3. Check that complete vertical circles are possible.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\alpha=3/7\).

(b)

\(T_B=36mg/7\).

(c)

The top tension is \(6mg/7\gt 0\); complete circles are possible.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\alpha\). The fall from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(2ac\), so \(v_B^2=ag(3+4c)\). At \(A\), \(T_A=mg(3-c)\), while at \(B\), \(T_B=mg(3+5c)\). The ratio gives \[3+5c=2(3-c),\] so \(7c=3\), giving \(c=3/7\).

Part (b)

Substitute \(c=3/7\) into \(T_B=mg(3+5c)\), giving \(T_B=36mg/7\). Also \(T_A=18mg/7\), confirming the ratio.

Part (c)

The energy constant \(v^2/(ag)+2y/a\) is \(3+6/7=27/7\). At the top, \(v^2/(ag)=27/7-2=13/7\), so the tension there is \(mg(13/7-1)=6mg/7\gt 0\). It is the minimum tension, and the top speed is positive.
questions.hint_html: Use the top of the circle for the global contact check, not just the two named points.

marking_criteria.description_html: Verify nonnegative minimum tension and positive speed.

questions.title: Two points ninety degrees apart
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves in complete vertical circles at the end of a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Relative to the centre, let \(P=(4a/5,3a/5)\) and \(Q=(3a/5,-4a/5)\). These radii are perpendicular. The speeds at \(P\) and \(Q\) are \(u\) and \(v\). The tension at \(Q\) is three times that at \(P\).

  1. Find a relation between \(u^2\) and \(v^2\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(u\).

    [5]

  3. Find the least tension during a complete revolution.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The fall from \(P\) to \(Q\) is \(3a/5+4a/5=7a/5\). Energy gives \(\frac12mv^2=\frac12mu^2+mg(7a/5)\), so \(v^2=u^2+14ag/5\).

Part (b)

At \(P\), \(T_P=mu^2/a-3mg/5\). At \(Q\), \(T_Q=mv^2/a+4mg/5\). Set \(q=u^2/(ag)\); part (a) then gives \(T_Q/(mg)=q+18/5\). The ratio requires \[q+\frac{18}{5}=3\left(q-\frac35\right),\] so \(q=27/10\). The speed is the positive square root.

Part (c)

The energy constant \(v^2/(ag)+2y/a\) is \(27/10+6/5=39/10\). The least tension occurs at the top, where \(T/(mg)=39/10-3=9/10\). It is positive, confirming the complete-circle assumption.
questions.hint_html: The radial component of weight changes sign between the two points.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find tension at Q with the opposite weight sign.
Use the top as the minimum-tension point.

questions.title: A complete circle with a cap on the contact force
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves inside a fixed smooth spherical shell of radius \(a\), in a vertical great circle. At a point whose radius makes an angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical, where \(\cos\theta=1/6\), its speed is \(v\). The particle must complete the circle without losing contact; the limiting zero-reaction case at the top is allowed.

  1. Find the least possible value of v.

    [4]

  2. The normal reaction is not to exceed \(8mg\) anywhere. Find the complete set of allowable values of \(v\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The height at the given point is \(a/6\), so the rise to the top is \(5a/6\). Hence \(v_{\rm top}^2=v^2-5ag/3\). At the top, \(N+mg=mv_{\rm top}^2/a\). Nonnegative reaction requires \(v_{\rm top}^2\ge ag\), giving \(v^2\ge8ag/3\). The least speed is its positive square root.

Part (b)

The energy constant \(K=v^2/(ag)+1/3\) gives normal reaction \(N/(mg)=K-3y/a\). It is greatest at the bottom, where \[\frac{N_{\max}}{mg}=\frac{v^2}{ag}+\frac{10}{3}.\] Thus the cap requires \(v^2/(ag)\le14/3\). Combine this with part (a), and take positive square roots. Both boundaries are included because the top limiting case and equality at the force cap are allowed.
questions.hint_html: The minimum contact force occurs at the top; the maximum occurs at the bottom.

marking_criteria.description_html: Locate the maximum reaction at the bottom.
Express it in terms of the given speed.

questions.title: Maximum and minimum tensions
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) completes vertical circles while attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). The greatest and least tensions are in the ratio \(5:2\). At a point where the string makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical, the speed is \(\sqrt{8ag}\).

  1. Find the greatest and least tensions.

    [3]

  2. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [3]

  3. Find the top speed and verify the complete-circle condition.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Energy between bottom and top gives a difference of \(4ag\) between their squared speeds. Their radial equations then give \(T_{\max}-T_{\min}=6mg\). Write the two tensions as \(5b\) and \(2b\). Then \(3b=6mg\), so \(b=2mg\), giving \(10mg\) and \(4mg\).

Part (b)

At the bottom, \(10mg-mg=mv_0^2/a\), so \(v_0^2=9ag\). At the stated point, the rise from the bottom is \(a(1-\cos\theta)\). Energy gives \(8ag=9ag-2ag(1-\cos\theta)\), so \(\cos\theta=1/2\).

Part (c)

Energy gives \(v_{\rm top}^2=9ag-4ag=5ag\). Thus the top speed is \(\sqrt{5ag}\), and its tension is \(m(5ag)/a-mg=4mg\gt 0\). Both the speed and the minimum tension are positive.
questions.hint_html: The tension difference between the bottom and top is 6mg, not 4mg.

questions.title: A quarter-circle rise from a lower point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially it is at \(A=(5a/13,-12a/13)\), using horizontal and upward axes through \(O\). It is projected tangentially anticlockwise with speed \(\sqrt{5ag}\). Let \(B\) be the point reached after the radius has turned through \(90^\circ\).

  1. Find the tension at B, checking that B is reached with the string taut.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The anticlockwise quarter turn gives \(B=(12a/13,5a/13)\). The rise is \(17a/13\). Energy gives \[v_B^2=5ag-2g\frac{17a}{13}=\frac{31}{13}ag.\] At \(B\), the inward component of weight is \(5mg/13\), so \[T_B+\frac5{13}mg=\frac{mv_B^2}{a},\qquad T_B=2mg.\] On this ascent the tension decreases continuously with height, so the positive value at \(B\), together with its positive speed, verifies the whole preceding arc is possible.
questions.hint_html: Rotate the coordinate pair by 90° before comparing heights.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check positive speed and tension on the preceding ascent.

questions.title: Reactions on a bead threaded on a circular wire
questions.prompt_html:
A bead of mass \(m\) is threaded on a fixed smooth circular wire of radius \(a\) in a vertical plane. Relative to its centre \(O\), let \(A=(3a/5,-4a/5)\) and \(B=(4a/5,3a/5)\). The bead travels up the intervening quarter-circle from \(A\) to \(B\). At \(A\) the wire reaction is inward. At \(B\) it is outward, with magnitude one eighth of the reaction at \(A\).

  1. Find the magnitude of the reaction at B.

    [4]

  2. Find \(k\) if \(v_A=\sqrt{kag}\), and verify that B is reached.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(R_B=rmg\), so the inward reaction at \(A\) is \(8rmg\). The radial equations give \[\frac{v_A^2}{ag}=8r-\frac45,\qquad \frac{v_B^2}{ag}=\frac35-r.\] The height rise is \(7a/5\), so energy gives \(v_A^2-v_B^2=14ag/5\). Therefore \(9r-7/5=14/5\), yielding \(r=7/15\).

Part (b)

From the first radial equation, \(k=8(7/15)-4/5=44/15\). The second gives \(v_B^2/(ag)=3/5-7/15=2/15\gt 0\). Speed squared decreases with height on the quarter-circle, so it remains positive before \(B\). A threaded bead is constrained to the wire even when the reaction changes sign; zero reaction is not a loss-of-contact rule for this model.
questions.hint_html: Treat the reaction as a signed radial force; the bead is threaded on the wire.

questions.title: Recovering two angle cosines from speeds and tensions
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially its position is above the centre, at upward radius-angle \(\theta\), and it is projected tangentially downwards with speed \(u=\sqrt{ag}\). At a later lower point, where the radius has acute angle \(\alpha\) to the downward vertical, its speed is \(\sqrt3\,u\) and its tension is five times the initial tension.

  1. Find the initial tension.

    [4]

  2. Find \(\cos\alpha\), and check that the stated lower point is reached before any slackening.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(T_A=3mg/4\).

(b)

\(\cos\alpha=3/4\); the descending arc has positive tension.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(d=\cos\alpha\). The squared speed increases from \(ag\) to \(3ag\), so energy gives \(c+d=1\). The initial tension is \(mg(1-c)\), and the later tension is \(mg(3+d)\). Hence \[3+d=5(1-c).\] Using \(d=1-c\), this gives \(4-c=5-5c\), so \(c=1/4\). Therefore \(T_A=3mg/4\).

Part (b)

From \(c+d=1\), \(d=3/4\). The energy constant is \(K=1+2c=3/2\). On the initial descent, the upward height cosine decreases from \(1/4\) to \(-3/4\), so the tension \(mg(K-3y/a)\) increases from \(3mg/4\) to \(15mg/4\). It stays positive, while speed increases, so the lower point is reached on the stated constrained arc.
questions.hint_html: Use the change in speed squared to obtain the sum of the two height cosines.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the energy constant or equivalent tension formula.
