questions.title: Testing a complete-circle condition
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves in complete vertical circles while attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Points \(A\) and \(B\) lie on the same side of the vertical through the centre. Their radii make the same acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward and upward verticals, respectively. The speed at the upper point \(B\) is \(\sqrt{2ag}\). The tension at \(A\) is four times the tension at \(B\). Let the speed at \(A\) be \(u\).

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\) and \(u\).

    [5]

  2. Verify that the complete-circle condition is satisfied.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\cos\theta=2/3\), \(\displaystyle u=\sqrt{14ag/3}\).

(b)

The top speed squared is \(4ag/3\), and the top tension is \(mg/3\gt 0\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(c=\cos\theta\). The rise from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(2ac\), so \(u^2=ag(2+4c)\). At the upper point \(T_B=mg(2-c)\), while at the lower point \(T_A=mg(2+5c)\). The ratio gives \[2+5c=4(2-c),\] so \(c=2/3\). Consequently \(u^2=ag(2+8/3)=14ag/3\).

Part (b)

From \(B\) to the top the additional rise is \(a(1-2/3)=a/3\). Thus \(v_{\rm top}^2=2ag-2ag/3=4ag/3\). The top radial equation gives \(T_{\rm top}=m(4ag/3)/a-mg=mg/3\gt 0\). The top is the minimum-speed and minimum-tension point, so the claimed complete motion is consistent.
questions.hint_html: After solving the ratio, test the point at the very top as well.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use energy from B to the top.

questions.title: Opposite points with a different global energy
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves in complete vertical circles at the end of a light inextensible string of length \(a\). The points \(A\) and \(B\) are opposite ends of a diameter. Point \(A\) is below the centre, with its radius at acute angle \(\theta\) to the downward vertical; \(B\) is above the centre. The speed at \(A\) is \(\sqrt{7ag}\), and \(T_A:T_B=3:1\).

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [4]

  2. Find the greatest speed and verify that the string remains taut for a complete turn.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\). Energy gives \(v_B^2=ag(7-4c)\). The radial equations give \(T_A=mg(7+c)\) and \(T_B=mg(7-5c)\). Therefore \(7+c=3(7-5c)\), so \(16c=14\) and \(c=7/8\).

Part (b)

The greatest speed is at the bottom, a further \(a(1-7/8)=a/8\) below \(A\). Hence \(v_{\max}^2=7ag+ag/4=29ag/4\), giving \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{29ag}/2\). At the top, the squared speed is \(29ag/4-4ag=13ag/4\), so the least tension is \(m(13ag/4)/a-mg=9mg/4\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html: The fastest point is not necessarily either of the two named points.

questions.title: A tension ratio at opposite ends of a diameter
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is joined to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It moves in a vertical circle. At a lower point \(A\), the radius makes an acute angle \(\theta\) to the downward vertical, with \(\cos\theta=1/3\), and the speed is \(\sqrt{6ag}\). Point \(B\) is diametrically opposite \(A\).

  1. Find \(T_A:T_B\).

    [4]

  2. Check whether complete vertical circular motion is possible.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The rise from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(2a/3\), so \(v_B^2=6ag-4ag/3=14ag/3\). At \(A\), \(T_A=mg(6+1/3)=19mg/3\). At \(B\), \(T_B=mg(14/3-1/3)=13mg/3\). Thus the ratio is \(19:13\).

Part (b)

The rise from \(A\) to the top is \(4a/3\), so the top speed squared is \(6ag-8ag/3=10ag/3\). Its tension is \(10mg/3-mg=7mg/3\gt 0\), and this is the minimum tension.
questions.hint_html: Gravity contributes with opposite signs in the two radial equations.

questions.title: An initial angle for a limiting complete circle
questions.prompt_html:
A particle is joined to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Initially the string makes an acute angle \(\theta\) with the downward vertical. The particle is projected tangentially upwards with speed \(3\sqrt{ag/2}\) and has just sufficient speed for a complete vertical circle, allowing zero tension at the top only.

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the top of a limiting complete circle, zero tension gives \(v_T^2=ag\). The rise from the starting point to the top is \(a(1+\cos\theta)\). Thus energy gives \[\frac92ag=ag+2ag(1+\cos\theta).\] Dividing by \(ag\) and rearranging yields \(2\cos\theta=3/2\), so \(\cos\theta=3/4\). This lies between zero and one. With this energy, tension is positive below the top and has its single limiting zero there.
questions.hint_html: At the top, just completing a string-constrained circle does not mean zero speed.

marking_criteria.description_html: Check the angle and limiting contact condition.

questions.title: A collision at the bottom of a spherical track
questions.prompt_html:
Two particles can move on the smooth inner surface of a fixed spherical shell of radius \(a\). Their motion is confined to one vertical great circle. Particle \(P\), of mass \(m\), starts at a horizontal end of a diameter and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{19ag/3}\). At the lowest point it collides directly with a stationary particle \(Q\) of mass \(4m\). Particle \(P\) rebounds. Particle \(Q\) has just enough speed after the collision to reach a point \(B\) at height \(2a/3\) above the lowest point, where it is instantaneously at rest. There is no horizontal external impulse during the collision.

  1. Find the velocities of P and Q immediately after collision, taking the incoming direction of P as positive.

    [5]

  2. Find the coefficient of restitution.

    [2]

  3. Find the cosine of the angle to the upward vertical at which P subsequently loses contact.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Before impact, energy gives \(U^2=19ag/3+2ag=25ag/3\), so \(U=5\sqrt{ag/3}\). To rise \(2a/3\), \(Q\) needs \(v_Q^2=2g(2a/3)=4ag/3\), and it moves in the positive direction. Horizontal momentum is conserved at the bottom: \[mU=mv_P+4mv_Q.\] Thus \(v_P=(5-8)\sqrt{ag/3}=-\sqrt{3ag}\), which is a rebound as stated.

Part (b)

Separation speed is \(v_Q-v_P=(2+3)\sqrt{ag/3}\). Approach speed is \(U=5\sqrt{ag/3}\). Their ratio is \(e=1\), within the physical range.

Part (c)

After impact, the new energy calculation must start with bottom speed squared \(3ag\). At height \(a\cos\theta\) above the centre, \[v^2=3ag-2ag(1+\cos\theta)=ag(1-2\cos\theta).\] At loss of contact the inward normal reaction is zero, so \(v^2=ag\cos\theta\). Therefore \(1-2\cos\theta=\cos\theta\), giving \(\cos\theta=1/3\). The speed squared at release is \(ag/3\gt 0\), and the reaction was positive earlier on this ascent. The collision must not be crossed by a single conservation-of-mechanical-energy equation.
questions.hint_html: Use energy on each smooth arc, but use momentum and restitution during impact.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the speed needed for Q’s rise.
Use the ratio of separation to approach speeds.
Set the normal reaction equal to zero.

questions.title: Coalescence at the lowest point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts with the string horizontal and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{8ag}\). At the lowest point it collides directly with a stationary particle of mass \(km\), where \(k\gt 0\), and the particles coalesce. There is no horizontal external impulse. The tension immediately after collision is \(7/11\) of its value immediately before collision.

  1. Find the speed and tension immediately before collision.

    [3]

  2. Find all possible values of k.

    [5]

  3. Determine whether the combined particle can complete a vertical circle in either case.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(U=\sqrt{10ag}\), \(T_-=11mg\).

(b)

\(k=1\) or \(k=4\).

(c)

It cannot complete a vertical circle in either case.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The fall to the bottom is \(a\), so \(U^2=8ag+2ag=10ag\). At the bottom the radial equation is \(T_--mg=mU^2/a\). Thus \(T_-=11mg\).

Part (b)

Let \(s=1+k\gt 1\). Momentum gives the common speed \(V=U/s\). The new tension is \[T_+=smg+\frac{smV^2}{a}=mg\left(s+\frac{10}{s}\right).\] The given ratio makes this equal to \(7mg\). Therefore \(s^2-7s+10=0\), so \(s=2\) or 5. Both exceed 1, giving \(k=1\) or 4. The coalescence reduces kinetic energy for both values.

Part (c)

A string-constrained complete circle needs bottom speed squared at least \(5ag\): energy removes \(4ag\) on reaching the top, where speed squared must still be at least \(ag\). Here \(V^2=10ag/s^2\), equal to \(5ag/2\) for \(s=2\) and \(2ag/5\) for \(s=5\). Both are below the threshold, so neither case gives complete circular motion.
questions.hint_html: After coalescence both the mass and the speed change in the radial equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the total mass in the post-collision radial equation.

questions.title: An elastic rebound just sufficient for a loop
questions.prompt_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts with the string horizontal and is projected vertically downwards with speed \(\sqrt{43ag}\). At the lowest point it collides directly and perfectly elastically with a stationary particle \(Q\) of mass \(km\). The particle \(P\) rebounds with just sufficient speed to complete a vertical circle in the limiting sense. No horizontal external impulse acts during the collision.

  1. Find the speed of P immediately before collision.

    [3]

  2. Find the velocity of P immediately after collision, taking its incoming direction as positive.

    [2]

  3. Find k.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The loss of potential energy is \(mga\). Hence \(\frac12mU^2=\frac12m(43ag)+mga\), so \(U^2=45ag\) and \(U=3\sqrt{5ag}\).

Part (b)

At the limiting top point, tension is zero and \(v_{\rm top}^2=ag\). Energy from the bottom to the top requires bottom speed squared \(ag+4ag=5ag\). Rebound makes the signed velocity \(-\sqrt{5ag}\). Zero tension at the single top instant is the limiting full-circle case, not a claim of an extended slack phase.

Part (c)

Put \(w=\sqrt{5ag}\). The incoming velocity is \(3w\) and the outgoing velocity of \(P\) is \(-w\). Perfect restitution gives \(v_Q-(-w)=3w\), so \(v_Q=2w\). Momentum gives \(3mw=-mw+km(2w)\), and therefore \(k=2\).
questions.hint_html: The limiting complete circle requires a nonzero speed at its highest point.

questions.title: A horizontal peg and a new circular path
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). Its initial position \(A\) is above and to the right of \(O\), with \(OA\) at an acute angle \(\alpha\) to the upward vertical. It is projected tangentially clockwise with speed \(\sqrt{ag}\). A small smooth peg \(B\) is \(a/4\) horizontally to the left of \(O\). When the string first becomes horizontal to the left, it catches the peg; the particle then moves on a circle centred at \(B\). On its first ascent in this smaller circle it reaches \(C\), above and to the left of \(B\), where the radius makes an angle \(\gamma\) with the upward vertical and \(\cos\gamma=3/5\). The tension at \(C\) equals that at the initial point \(A\).

  1. Find the speed squared when the string first catches the peg.

    [3]

  2. Find \(\cos\alpha\).

    [6]

  3. Check that C is reached before the string becomes slack in the smaller circle.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_0^2=ag(1+2\cos\alpha)\).

(b)

\(\cos\alpha=2/5\).

(c)

In the smaller circle slackening occurs at cosine \(4/5\), after C.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The catch point is \((-a,0)\), whereas \(A\) has height \(a\cos\alpha\). The string tension does no work on the arc. Energy gives \[\frac12mv_0^2=\frac12mag+mga\cos\alpha,\] so \(v_0^2=ag(1+2\cos\alpha)\). The tangent is vertical at the catch, for both circles, so the speed is continuous there.

Part (b)

Put \(c=\cos\alpha\). At \(A\), \(T_A=mg(1-c)\). After catching the peg the effective radius is \(r=3a/4\). The point \(C\) is \((3a/4)(3/5)=9a/20\) above the catch level, so \[\frac{v_C^2}{ag}=1+2c-\frac9{10}.\] At \(C\), \(T_C+3mg/5=mv_C^2/(3a/4)\). Therefore \[\frac{T_C}{mg}=\frac43(1+2c)-\frac95.\] Equate this to \(1-c\): \((11/3)c=22/15\), giving \(c=2/5\). Both tensions are then \(3mg/5\).

Part (c)

With \(c=2/5\), the catch speed squared is \(9ag/5\). At a point whose radius from \(B\) has upward cosine \(z\), the tension is \[\frac{T}{mg}=\frac{9ag/5}{(3a/4)g}-3z=\frac{12}{5}-3z.\] It is zero at \(z=4/5\). During the first ascent \(z\) increases from zero; \(C\) has \(z=3/5\lt 4/5\). Its speed squared is \(9ag/10\gt 0\), so it is reached with positive tension.
questions.hint_html: Use a new radius and a new centre after the peg is caught; do not change the speed discontinuously.

Obtain the speed and note continuity at the catch.

questions.title: A vertical peg and a jump in tension
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts below and to the right of \(O\), with the string at an acute angle \(\theta\) to the downward vertical. It is projected tangentially downwards with speed \(\frac12\sqrt{3ag}\). At the lowest point the string catches a small smooth peg \(A\), situated \(a/2\) vertically below \(O\). It then rises in a circle about \(A\). The string first becomes slack when the new radius makes angle \(\theta\) with the upward vertical through \(A\).

  1. Find \(\cos\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Find the ratio of the tensions immediately before and immediately after the string catches the peg.

    [3]

  3. Find the speed when the string becomes slack.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\). The original starting height relative to \(O\) is \(-ac\). At the bottom the speed squared is \(ag(3/4+2(1-c))=ag(11/4-2c)\). The new radius is \(a/2\). At release the rise from the common lowest point is \((a/2)(1+c)\), so \[v_L^2=ag(11/4-2c)-ag(1+c)=ag(7/4-3c).\] Zero tension in the smaller circle gives \(v_L^2=(ag/2)c\). Equating yields \(7/4=(7/2)c\), and therefore \(c=1/2\).

Part (b)

At the catch, \(v^2=ag(11/4-1)=7ag/4\). The speed is unchanged but the radius halves. Thus \[T_-=mg+\frac{mv^2}{a}=\frac{11}{4}mg,\qquad T_+=mg+\frac{mv^2}{a/2}=\frac92mg.\] Their ratio is \(11:18\).

Part (c)

At zero tension, \(v_L^2=(ag/2)\cos\theta=ag/4\). Hence \(v_L=\sqrt{ag}/2\). This is positive, and tension decreases from \(9mg/2\) to zero on the specified ascent, so the first loss condition is valid.
questions.hint_html: The force can change abruptly at the peg even though the speed does not.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the speed at the catch using energy.

questions.title: Two particles at the ends of a light rigid rod
questions.prompt_html:
Two particles \(P\) and \(Q\), each of mass \(m\), are attached to the ends of a light rigid rod of length \(4a\). The rod is smoothly pivoted at \(O\), with \(OQ=x\) and \(OP=4a-x\), where \(0\lt x\lt 4a\). At an instant when the rod is vertical with \(P\) above \(O\), particle \(P\) has horizontal speed \(u\). When the rod has turned through \(60^\circ\), the speed of \(P\) is \(3\sqrt{ag/2}\). At this latter instant both portions of the rod are in tension and these two tensions are equal. The rod has negligible mass; include the kinetic energy of both particles.

  1. Express the speed of Q at the latter instant in terms of x, a and g.

    [2]

  2. Find x.

    [5]

  3. Find u.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The two particles have the same instantaneous angular speed. Thus \(v_Q/x=v_P/(4a-x)\), so \(v_Q=3x\sqrt{ag/2}/(4a-x)\).

Part (b)

Put \(p=4a-x\). At \(60^\circ\), \(P\) is above the centre and \(Q\) is below it. The two inward equations are \[T_P+\frac12mg=\frac{m(9ag/2)}p,\qquad T_Q-\frac12mg=\frac{m(9ag/2)x}{p^2}.\] Using \(T_P=T_Q\) gives \((9a/2)(p-x)=p^2\). Write \(z=x/a\), so \((9/2)(4-2z)=(4-z)^2\). Hence \(z^2+z-2=0\), giving \(z=1\) or \(-2\). Only \(z=1\) lies in the allowed interval. Thus \(x=a\), and both tensions equal \(mg\gt 0\).

Part (c)

Now \(OP=3a\) and \(OQ=a\), so \(v_Q=v_P/3\) at all instants. During the turn, \(P\) falls by \(3a/2\) while \(Q\) rises by \(a/2\); the net potential-energy loss is \(mga\). Thus \[\frac12m\left(\frac{9ag}{2}+\frac{ag}{2}\right)-\frac12m\left(u^2+\frac{u^2}{9}\right)=mga.\] This gives \(5u^2/9=3ag/2\), hence \(u^2=27ag/10\). Initially the force in \(OP\) is compressive, of magnitude \(mg/10\); a rigid rod can supply this, unlike a string. No moment-of-inertia formula is required.
questions.hint_html: A light rigid rod can push as well as pull. Use the energies of the two particles, not a moment of inertia of a massive rod.
